St. George Utah Temple

Location
St. George, Utah. The temple stands at 250 East 400 South on a 6.5-acre site near the city's historic district, a white landmark among the red sandstone buttes of southern Utah.

Temple Number
First among the Church's operating temples. It is the oldest operating temple of the Church and the first temple dedicated in Utah.

Announced
January 31, 1871, by Brigham Young in a meeting with the St. George Stake high council and other local leaders, the first temple proposed since the exodus from Nauvoo. Erastus Snow answered the news with a shout of "Glory, hallelujah!"

Groundbreaking
November 9, 1871. Brigham Young dedicated the site, and excavation began the same day.

Dedicated
April 6 to 8, 1877, with the dedicatory prayer offered by President Daniel H. Wells of the First Presidency in the opening session of general conference, held in the temple; Brigham Young presided and, despite failing health, offered brief remarks. Portions were dedicated January 1, 1877: the baptistry by Wilford Woodruff, an assembly room by Erastus Snow, and a sealing room by Brigham Young Jr. Baptisms for the dead began January 9 and endowments January 11, 1877.

Rededicated
November 11 to 12, 1975, by President Spencer W. Kimball following a major expansion, and again on December 10, 2023, by President Jeffrey R. Holland, Acting President of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles, in two sessions.

Architecture
Truman O. Angell, architect, appointed by Brigham Young. Native red sandstone quarried north of the city and plastered white, rising 175 feet, with 143,969 square feet of floor area following the 2019 to 2023 renovation.

Ordinance Rooms
Three instruction rooms with a separate veil room, seventeen sealing rooms, and a baptistry whose font bowl and oxen are the originals from 1877.

First Temple President
Wilford Woodruff, later President of the Church. Under Brigham Young's direction, he and others made the first written record of temple ordinances that had previously been passed on by word of mouth.

Construction Story
  • Early Saints packed the site with volcanic rock, using a cannon as a pile driver to compact the foundation.
  • The temple was built by local craftsmen from local materials. Stone and lime for plaster came from nearby quarries, timber came from Mount Trumbull, Arizona, which required building a new road, and window glass and metal for nails and the roof came from Salt Lake City.
  • Brigham Young personally paid for the baptismal font. Cast in six pieces at the Davis and Howe foundry in Salt Lake City, it traveled by rail to Nephi and then by ox team through the summer heat. A freighter recalled that Orson Hyde, seeing the font in place, "came out weeping with joy."
  • Members of the Paiute tribes, on whose historic homeland St. George sits, participated in the construction and in early ordinance work.
  • A few construction workers left signatures and time capsules in the walls; one contained original poetry they had written. St. George had roughly 1,100 residents when the work began.

Changes Over Time
  • The temple has been renovated more than 10 times since 1877.
  • Lightning damaged the original tower in August 1878. A taller replacement designed by architect William H. Folsom was completed in 1883, and in 1994 the wooden tower was replaced with one of fiberglass and metal.
  • A 1917 project enlarged the annex, and a 1938 remodel moved the endowment rooms from the basement to the main level, replacing a large assembly room with smaller mural rooms. Architects Don Carlos Young and Ramm Hansen designed both.
  • A 1975 renovation by Church architect Emil Fetzer nearly doubled the temple's 56,062 square feet, added sealing rooms, and replaced the live-acted endowment with the film presentation. President Spencer W. Kimball rededicated the temple that November.
  • The temple closed November 4, 2019, for a four-year renovation: exterior walls reinforced with a two-inch layer of gunite and steel, all mechanical, electrical, and plumbing systems replaced, north and west additions rebuilt to match the original architecture, a bride's exit and an independent baptistry entrance added, and interior finishes returned to 19th-century design patterns.

Symbolism & Design
  • Brigham Young's plan closely followed Joseph Smith's designs for the Nauvoo Temple, carrying that earlier pattern across generations.
  • The red sandstone walls are plastered white, setting the temple apart from the surrounding red rock country.
  • The exterior pairs an octagonal tower and domed cupola with rows of arched and circular windows and white Tuscan columns.
  • The 2019 to 2023 renovation restored the interior to its 1870s and 1880s design period, with new murals by local artists and decorative fixtures matched to designs from a World's Fair catalog.

Trivia
  • It is the only temple completed during Brigham Young's presidency.
  • It was the first temple where the endowment was performed by proxy for the dead. Wilford Woodruff recorded almost 25,000 baptisms for the dead, 12,000 endowments, and 3,800 sealings in the first year alone.
  • A stretch of road between Arizona settlements and St. George was nicknamed "the Honeymoon Trail" because so many couples traveled it to be married in the temple.
  • Almost 670,000 visitors toured the temple during its fall 2023 open house.

Syracuse Utah Temple

Location
Syracuse, Utah. The temple stands on a 12.268-acre site at 1098 South 2500 West, surrounded by farmland between the Great Salt Lake and Interstate 15, about 30 miles northwest of Salt Lake City, at an elevation of 4,275 feet.

Temple Number
The Church's 206th dedicated temple. At its dedication it was the 24th temple dedicated in Utah and the third built in Davis County, following the Bountiful Utah Temple (1995) and the Layton Utah Temple (2024).

Announced
April 5, 2020, by President Russell M. Nelson, in the Sunday afternoon session of a general conference broadcast from Temple Square without a congregation because of the COVID-19 pandemic. It was one of eight temples announced that day, a list that also included Dubai, United Arab Emirates, and Shanghai, People's Republic of China.

Groundbreaking
June 12, 2021. Elder Kevin R. Duncan, General Authority Seventy, presided at the ceremony and offered the site dedicatory prayer.

Dedicated
June 8, 2025, by President Russell M. Nelson, in a single session at 4 p.m., accompanied by Elder Quentin L. Cook of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles. The service was broadcast to meetinghouses throughout the temple district.

Architecture
A three-story steel-frame structure clad in white Moncini granite, with 90,526 square feet of floor area rising 219 feet 8 inches to the top of its single attached end spire.

Ordinance Rooms
Four instruction rooms, four sealing rooms, and two baptistries.

First Temple President
Val Dean Steel, with Luann Kay Flint Steel as matron. Their calls were announced in November 2024, and they began serving at the temple's dedication.

Construction Story
  • The site was announced on August 28, 2020: a 12-acre field at the intersection of 2500 West and 1025 South, still surrounded by working farms. The official exterior rendering followed on February 16, 2021, showing a three-story building of roughly 89,000 square feet.
  • Elder Kevin R. Duncan, who presided at the groundbreaking, grew up on this ground, and his great-grandfather was the first bishop of Syracuse. "I am very familiar with these fields where we stand, where we are gathered today," he said at the ceremony. "From this temple site, I can see the barn roof of my childhood home."
  • The temple was announced in part to ease demand on the Ogden Utah Temple, which was then serving members of 63 stakes. At the announcement, Utah was home to 2.1 million Church members, roughly two-thirds of the state's population.
  • Materials crossed the Atlantic in both directions: the exterior granite was fabricated by Campolonghi of Montignoso, Italy, and installed by IMS Masonry of Lindon, Utah, while the art glass was fabricated by Progetto Arte Poli of Verona, Italy, and installed by Steel Encounters of Salt Lake City.
  • The open house began with a media day on May 7, 2025, followed by tours for invited guests, then a public open house from May 10 to May 31, 2025, excluding Sundays.

Symbolism & Design
  • Design motifs feature the flora of the Great Salt Lake and its nearby wetlands, including the snowball sand-verbena, desert paintbrush, common cattail, and reeds, rendered in shades of blues, greens, golds, yellows, and reds drawn from the area's indigenous plants.
  • The transitioning greens, blues, and yellows in the art glass represent reflections of the lake, a nod to Syracuse's identity as the "Gateway to Antelope Island." The glass features faceted crystal and was designed by Architectural Nexus with assistance from Holdman Studios.
  • Millwork and stain-grade doors are plain sawn sapele, the celestial room carpet is 100 percent New Zealand wool, and the crystal chandeliers were fabricated by Schonbek of Plattsburgh, New York.

Trivia
  • It was the first temple in the Church dedicated with two baptismal fonts. "The reason for that is the high concentration of members and especially high concentration of youth," Elder Kevin R. Duncan explained during the open house. "Now they can come more frequently."
  • Its dedication marked the 200th temple to open its doors during President Russell M. Nelson's 100-year life, and it was the fifth temple he personally dedicated: Sapporo Japan as President of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles, then Concepción Chile, Rome Italy, Deseret Peak Utah, and Syracuse as Church President.
  • The Church's first ward in Syracuse was created on December 1, 1895, nearly 130 years before the city received a temple. The temple's district comprises 16 northern Davis County stakes in Syracuse, West Point, Clearfield, Clinton, and Sunset.

- Evan

Vernal Utah Temple

Location
Vernal, Utah, on 1.6 acres two blocks south of Main Street in the Ashley Valley.

Temple Number
The 51st dedicated temple.

Announced
February 13, 1994, when local leaders told members the historic Uintah Stake Tabernacle would become a house of the Lord.

Groundbreaking
May 13, 1995. President Gordon B. Hinckley presided.

Dedicated
November 2 to 4, 1997, by President Gordon B. Hinckley, in eleven sessions. About 3,528 people attended the first session.

Architecture
FFKR Architects of Salt Lake City, with Roger Jackson as chief architect, working inside the brick shell of the 1907 tabernacle. Face brick, one of the few temples without a light colored exterior. 38,771 square feet, rising 98 feet.

Ordinance Rooms
Two instruction rooms in a two stage progressive arrangement, three sealing rooms, one baptistry.

First Temple President
Alva C. Snow.

Construction Story
  • This was the first temple built from an existing building. The Uintah Stake Tabernacle, dedicated August 24, 1907, by President Joseph F. Smith, had fallen into serious disrepair and had not hosted a stake conference since 1983.
  • The interior was removed entirely. As the project put it, they kept the outside and built a new building inside.
  • About 1,500 crumbling bricks in the outer wall had to be replaced, and matching brick no longer existed. The answer was the Reader Home, a turn of the century house in Vernal whose brick had come from the same kiln as the tabernacle's, the Abner N. Swain Brickworks. Crews spent two months taking roughly 16,000 bricks out of the house by hand.
  • The public open house ran October 11 through 25, 1997, and drew about 118,700 visitors.

Symbolism & Design
  • A historic plaque describes the tabernacle's form as a simplified and almost civic variant of the Georgian New England church. The temple kept that form deliberately.
  • The west tower was rebuilt to the original specifications, and a matching tower was raised at the east end, where the tabernacle never had one.
  • The angel Moroni statue was placed on that new east tower on September 16, 1996. It went up painted gold; four months later the decision was made to give it the traditional gold leaf finish instead.
  • The building carries two dates, 1907 and 1997, the years it was dedicated as a tabernacle and then as a temple.
  • The celestial room armchairs are replicas, in horsehair fabric, of the chairs used by the First Presidency and the Quorum of the Twelve in the Salt Lake Temple.

Trivia
  • It stood as the only temple made from an existing tabernacle for nearly two decades, until the Provo City Center Temple was dedicated in 2016.
  • President Gordon B. Hinckley both broke ground for the temple and dedicated it, two and a half years apart.

Washington D.C. Temple

Location
Kensington, Maryland. The temple carries the name of the capital it serves, but the building itself stands in suburban Kensington, Maryland, on a 52-acre site about 10 miles north of the U.S. Capitol. It rises in full view of the Capital Beltway (I-495), where millions of drivers have seen it since 1974.

Temple Number
The Church's 16th operating temple at its dedication, the first built in the Eastern United States and the Church's first east of the Mississippi River since the 1840s.

Announced
November 15, 1968. Ground was broken on the Kensington site just over three weeks later.

Groundbreaking
December 7, 1968. President Hugh B. Brown of the First Presidency presided. Full construction began May 28, 1971.

Dedicated
November 19, 1974, by President Spencer W. Kimball, in ten sessions held over four days through November 22, attended by some 40,000 members from across the eastern United States and eastern Canada.

Rededicated
August 14, 2022, by President Russell M. Nelson, in three sessions, following a renovation that had closed the temple since March 2018.

Architecture
Fred L. Markham, Henry P. Fetzer, Harold K. Beecher, and Keith W. Wilcox, architects, working under Church architect Emil B. Fetzer. Six-spire reinforced concrete structure sheathed in 173,000 square feet of Alabama white marble, 248 feet long by 136 feet wide, rising 288 feet to the top of the angel Moroni statue, with 156,558 square feet of floor area. It has been the tallest temple in the Church since its dedication.

Ordinance Rooms
Six instruction rooms, ten sealing rooms, and a baptistry with the font resting on twelve oxen representing the tribes of Israel.

First Temple President
Edward E. Drury Jr., a former Denver stake president who had just been released as president of the Delaware-Maryland Mission, called in 1973 ahead of the temple's 1974 opening.

Construction Story
  • The temple was announced on November 15, 1968, and the site broken three weeks later, but full construction waited until May 28, 1971. The finished building cost approximately $15 million, furnishings included.
  • The seven-week public open house in the fall of 1974 drew 758,328 visitors, breaking the record of 662,401 set by the Los Angeles California Temple. Demand for tickets forced organizers to expand from two phone lines to seventeen.
  • First Lady Betty Ford toured on September 11, 1974, and called the visit "a really, truly great experience." Vice President Nelson Rockefeller and Chief Justice Warren Burger also walked through before the dedication.
  • The Church held its largest news conference to date on the temple's 878-foot enclosed walkway bridge, with more than 100 reporters attending; coverage ultimately ran to 1,374 articles in 931 newspapers across all 50 states.

Changes Over Time
  • The temple closed March 5, 2018, for a renovation lasting more than four years: energy-efficient mechanical, electrical, and lighting systems, new plumbing, refreshed finishes and furnishings, and improved grounds.
  • Pandemic delays pushed the reopening celebration to 2022. The public open house ran April 28 to June 11, 2022, was extended to meet demand, and drew almost 350,000 guests, including U.S. senators, Supreme Court justices, and foreign ambassadors.
  • President Nelson, who rededicated the temple in 2022, had himself attended the original dedication in 1974.

Symbolism & Design
  • The six spires deliberately echo the Salt Lake Temple. Per the design intent the Church has published, the Salt Lake Temple represented the foundation of the Church and the Washington D.C. Temple its international future.
  • The spires are finished in 24-karat gold, and the 18-foot gold-leafed bronze angel Moroni by sculptor Avard T. Fairbanks makes this one of five temples whose Moroni statue holds the gold plates.
  • The exterior marble came from the quarry at Sylacauga, Alabama, and the windows combine stained glass with panels of translucent marble.

Trivia
  • Washington radio personalities came to use the temple as a reference point when announcing Beltway traffic, a sign it had taken its place among the monuments of the capital.
  • Since the 1970s the phrase "SURRENDER DOROTHY" has appeared again and again on the CSX railroad bridge that crosses the Beltway near the temple, a Wizard of Oz joke likening the temple's spires to the Emerald City. Highway crews repeatedly removed it, and in 2018 the bridge briefly read "SURRENDER DONALD" instead.
  • During the 1974 open house, President Spencer W. Kimball offered the invocation in the U.S. Senate and Elder Gordon B. Hinckley did the same in the House of Representatives on back-to-back days.

Albuquerque New Mexico Temple

Location
Albuquerque, New Mexico. An 8.5-acre site at 10301 San Francisco Road NE, on the northeast heights of the city at an elevation of 5,729 feet, with the Sandia Mountains rising directly to the east.

Temple Number
The 73rd dedicated temple in operation, and the first built in New Mexico.

Announced
April 4, 1997, by Gordon B. Hinckley.

Groundbreaking
June 20, 1998, presided over by Lynn A. Mickelsen of the Seventy, then president of the North America Southwest Area.

Dedicated
March 5, 2000, by Gordon B. Hinckley, in four sessions attended by more than 13,500 Latter-day Saints.

Architecture
Fanning Bard Tatum Architects of Albuquerque. Desert Rose precast concrete with Texas Pearl granite at the base, 34,245 square feet, with a single attached end spire carrying the angel Moroni.

Ordinance Rooms
Two instruction rooms, three sealing rooms, and one baptistry.

Construction Story
  • The public open house ran February 17 to February 26, 2000, nine days, and drew roughly 70,000 visitors.
  • The mountains the temple was sited against turned out to have an opinion about the front door. The original hinged entrance doors were replaced with glass sliding doors because of the winds coming off the Sandias.

Symbolism & Design
  • The exterior was chosen to answer the landscape rather than stand apart from it. The Desert Rose concrete and Texas Pearl granite read pink in the evening light, which is exactly what the Sandia range does at sunset, a color the mountains are named for.
  • Church News described the building as the first of its design in the Church, and framed the temple as a meeting point for a region where three cultures come together: American Indian, Hispanic and Anglo.

Changes Over Time
  • A 2019 renovation converted the original kitchen and cafeteria into office space, a change made across many temples of this era as patron meal service was discontinued.

Trivia
  • The temple stands at 5,729 feet above sea level, on the high desert bench that runs up toward the mountains from the Rio Grande.
  • It arrived in a crowded season. The Church's May 2000 conference report covered seven temple dedications in a single article, Albuquerque among them.

Burley Idaho Temple

Location
Burley, Idaho. A 10.12-acre site at 40 South 150 East, in the Magic Valley farming country of south central Idaho.

Temple Number
The 212th dedicated temple in operation, and the seventh dedicated in Idaho.

Announced
April 4, 2021, by Russell M. Nelson at the close of the 191st Annual General Conference.

Groundbreaking
June 4, 2022, presided over by Brent H. Nielson of the Presidency of the Seventy.

Dedicated
January 11, 2026, by Dallin H. Oaks. It was the first temple he dedicated as President of the Church, and the first dedication of 2026.

Architecture
Naylor Wentworth Lund Architects. A two-story steel frame clad in Bianco Sardo granite, fabricated in Millcreek, Utah. 45,300 square feet, 172 feet to the top of a single attached end spire.

Ordinance Rooms
Four instruction rooms, three sealing rooms, and one baptistry.

Construction Story
  • The ground it stands on was given. Leroy Funk and his siblings donated farmland their family had worked for decades. Funk put the credit elsewhere: "It is here because of the faithful ones who came before."
  • Latter-day Saints have been in the Burley area since 1879. The first branch, fourteen members, was organized in a log cabin in May 1880.
  • The public open house ran November 6 to November 22, 2025, through a stretch of unseasonably warm and sunny weather that had the tour coordinators joking about handing out sunscreen in November.

Symbolism & Design
  • The art glass is drawn from the crop the valley is known for. Its patterns are the blossoms and leaves of the potato plant, with the sugar beet fields of the Magic Valley informing the wider design.
  • The color palette was taken from the farmland and the open sky above it: blue, gold, amber, cream, orange, peach and green.
  • Interior stonework is Botticino Classico marble with Jerusalem Gold and Verde Guatemala accents, and the artwork inside was commissioned around the local landscape and the early Latter-day Saints of Burley.

Trivia
  • President Oaks chose Burley for his first dedication as President of the Church because of where he grew up. He lived in nearby Twin Falls as a boy for about five years, and said the place was "close to my heart."
  • The drive to the temple went from about 45 minutes to about five. Before Burley, members here attended the Twin Falls Idaho Temple.
  • Susan Young, Twin Falls temple matron from 2016 to 2019, remembered Burley youth arriving for baptisms at 3:30 in the morning, week after week. The baptistry would be full of young people sitting in white, and quiet enough to hear a pin drop.
  • The open house was run to be reachable: 143 tours in Spanish, nine in American Sign Language, and one tactile tour for visitors who needed it.

Cody Wyoming Temple

Status
Under construction. The public open house runs August 27 through September 12, 2026, excluding Sundays, and admission is free with no reservation required. Dedication is scheduled for Sunday, October 25, 2026.

Location
555 Temple View Lane, Cody, Wyoming. A 4.69-acre site northwest of Skyline Drive at Cody Canal, in the northwestern corner of the state near the Montana border, at an elevation of 5,134 feet with Heart Mountain on the horizon.

Temple Number
The third temple built in Wyoming, following Star Valley in 2016 and Casper in 2024. Its number among dedicated temples will be fixed at dedication.

Announced
October 3, 2021, by President Russell M. Nelson, at the October 2021 general conference, among thirteen temples announced that session.

Groundbreaking
September 27, 2024. Elder Steven R. Bangerter, First Counselor in the North America Central Area Presidency, presided and offered the site dedicatory prayer. Elder Kevin R. Duncan, Executive Director of the Temple Department, also attended.

Architecture
A single-story building of 9,950 square feet, 101 feet to the top of the spire. The exterior is precast concrete panels. A single attached central tower rises as a multi-tiered steeple capped with a gold pyramidal spire. The official exterior rendering was released March 27, 2023.

Ordinance Rooms
One instruction room, one sealing room, and one baptistry.

Construction Story
  • The site was announced in March 2023 as an empty field northwest of Skyline Drive, roughly seventeen months after the temple itself was announced.
  • Modular construction methods carried the project at unusual speed, with the exterior essentially finished about eighteen months after work began.
  • In his site dedicatory prayer, Elder Bangerter asked a blessing on the surrounding community rather than only on the Church membership, praying that neighbors would feel a spirit of peace and that the temple's presence would bring added joy, prosperity, beauty, and unity to their lives.

Symbolism & Design
  • The gold pyramidal spire replaces the angel Moroni statue found on many older temples, a choice increasingly common among the small single-story temples built in this era.
  • At 9,950 square feet, Cody is built to the scale of its community rather than to the scale of a regional temple. The single instruction room and single sealing room are the design's honest statement about who it is for.

Trivia
  • Nearly 67,000 Latter-day Saints live in Wyoming, meeting in more than 170 congregations, roughly one in every nine residents of the state.
  • Members in northwest Wyoming currently travel to the Billings Montana Temple. Cody will end that drive for them.
  • Cody is already home to the Historic Cody Mural and Museum, a Church meetinghouse whose domed ceiling carries a large mural depicting the Restoration and the westward migration. The chapel and visitors' center are open to the public during summer months.
  • Wyoming's pioneer connection is not incidental. Latter-day Saint companies crossed the state throughout the 1840s to 1860s on their way to the Salt Lake Valley.

- Evan

Kirtland Temple

Location
Kirtland, Ohio, at 9020 Chillicothe Road. The building stands on a bluff about 25 miles east of Cleveland, overlooking the Chagrin Valley.

Status
Not an operating temple. It is preserved as a historic site and open to visitors of any faith at no charge, with guided tours beginning at the adjacent visitors' center. No ordinances are performed there, so it has no temple number, no temple district, and no temple president.

Announced
December 27, 1832. A revelation recorded that day, now Doctrine and Covenants 88, directed the Saints in Kirtland to establish a house of prayer, fasting, faith, learning, glory, order, and God.

Construction Begun
June 5, 1833. The cornerstones were laid on July 23, 1833.

Dedicated
March 27, 1836, by Joseph Smith. The service was repeated several days later for those who could not be seated the first time.

Architecture
No professional architect. The First Presidency of the day, Joseph Smith, Sidney Rigdon, and Frederick G. Williams, reported receiving the design by vision in 1833, and the plan called for an interior 55 feet wide by 65 feet long. The walls are locally quarried sandstone laid as rubble masonry, finished in stucco and scored to imitate cut coursed stone. Roughly 15,000 square feet across three levels. The exterior follows the New England Protestant meetinghouse form with Federal and Gothic elements: lancet windows along the sides, ten small dormers lighting the attic story, and a bell tower over the front.

Construction Story
  • The walls were supposed to be brick. Frederick G. Williams supervised brick production from April to September 1833, but the crews had no experience and the bricks were unusable. The effort was abandoned by mid-September, leaving a finished stone foundation with nothing to build on top of it.
  • The fix came from Artemus Millet, a Canadian convert with experience on mills, chimneys, and foundations, who reached Kirtland in late October 1833. Noting how much sandstone the local quarries held, he proposed rubble masonry walls under a stucco finish, which is how the temple was actually built. Most retellings credit Brigham Young with recruiting him. Millet's own reminiscence and Hyrum Smith's papers say the written request came from Hyrum.
  • Zion's Camp emptied the site in the summer of 1834. Heber C. Kimball later recalled that only ten or fifteen men were left in Kirtland, and that at times no more than five or six were working on the building.
  • When the design was presented in June 1833, Hyrum Smith ran home for a scythe to start clearing the wheat field on the building site. Asked by his mother where he was going with it, he said he was "determined to be the first at the work."
  • What the temple cost was never settled. Ira Ames took over the building committee's books and found them in disorder. Scholarly estimates range from $30,000 to $100,000, with a figure near $40,000 the most commonly cited.

Historical Significance
  • This was the first temple the Latter Day Saints completed. Its formal name was the House of the Lord. The word temple was not yet in general use, and Joseph Smith's records also refer to the building as the Chapel.
  • The dedication set a pattern later dedications still follow. Joseph Smith read a prayer he had received by revelation, now Doctrine and Covenants 109, the congregation gave the Hosanna Shout, and they sang "The Spirit of God," which William W. Phelps wrote for the occasion. All three became standard elements of temple dedications afterward.
  • On April 3, 1836, one week after the dedication, Joseph Smith and Oliver Cowdery recorded a vision at the pulpits in which Moses, Elias, and Elijah conferred priesthood keys. The account is published as Doctrine and Covenants 110, and Latter-day Saints trace the authority for temple sealings and family history work to it.
  • The building functioned as a school as much as a meetinghouse. As many as 140 people studied reading, writing, history, geography, and Hebrew grammar in the third-floor rooms during the week.

Ownership History
  • A financial crisis struck Kirtland a year after the dedication. A dissenting faction led by Warren Parrish tried to seize the building, an unknown arsonist later tried to burn it, and most of the Saints left Ohio for Missouri in 1837 and 1838.
  • In 1880 an Ohio court recognized the heirs of Joseph Smith as holding title. About two decades later the Reorganized Church of Jesus Christ of Latter Day Saints, now Community of Christ, secured ownership through a legal claim of continuous use, and cared for the building from then until 2024.
  • On March 5, 2024, ownership transferred to The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. Discussions had begun in June 2021. The agreement totaled $192.5 million and covered the temple along with historic buildings in Nauvoo, manuscripts, and artifacts, with no value assigned to any single item. Community of Christ stated the proceeds would fund its mission priorities worldwide. The building closed for twenty days and reopened for free public tours on March 25, 2024.

Changes Over Time
  • After the Saints left, the temple served as a venue for private worship and public functions, and was leased for many years as a public school.
  • Community of Christ's predecessor restored the building as closely as possible to its original condition after establishing ownership.
  • The Historic American Buildings Survey documented the temple and its interior plan in 1934. It was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1969 and designated a National Historic Landmark in December 1976.

Trivia
  • The gilt inscription across the front reads House of the Lord, Built by the Church of Christ, 1834, dated two years before the building was finished.
  • The exterior stucco has crushed crockery, china, and glass mixed into it, which makes the walls catch the light. Children gathered the discarded shards. The often repeated story that the women of Kirtland deliberately broke their good china for the purpose has no known historical account behind it.
  • Both main halls carry two sets of tiered pulpits, one at each end, lettered in gilt with initials designating priesthood offices. The pews were built with movable benches so a congregation could face either direction.
  • Truman O. Angell worked here as a carpenter and joiner. He went on to serve as Church architect and to plan the Salt Lake Temple.

Logan Utah Temple

Location
Logan, Utah. Nine acres occupying an entire city block on an elevated bench of ancient Lake Bonneville, visible for miles across Cache Valley.

Temple Number
The fourth Latter-day Saint temple built, the second still in operation, and the second dedicated in Utah Territory.

Announced
October 6, 1876, by Brigham Young, at the 46th Semiannual General Conference. Young announced a temple for Cache Valley and divided Utah Territory into three temple districts. A letter that December named Logan as the site.

Groundbreaking
May 18, 1877. Elder Orson Pratt dedicated the site; President John W. Young broke ground. Less than a month after ground was broken at Manti, the first time in Church history that two temple groundbreakings fell in the same year.

Dedicated
May 17–19, 1884, by President John Taylor, in three sessions. The only temple John Taylor ever dedicated. Logan officials tidied the city, organized food and lodging for travelers, and ran excursion trains at reduced fare. About 1,500 people attended the first session.

Rededicated
March 13–15, 1979, by President Spencer W. Kimball, in nine sessions.

Architecture
Truman O. Angell, Church architect. Castellated style, shared with the Manti temple. Charles O. Card served as superintendent of construction, John Parry as master mason, William Davis as plastering foreman. The exterior is dark siliceous limestone, with buff-colored limestone reserved for detailed carving because it worked more easily. Five stories, 168 by 224 feet, 86 feet to the roofline. A domed cupola sits above each short end. The east tower rises 170 feet and the west 165, with four octagonal towers at 100 feet each. Originally 59,130 square feet, now 115,507.

Ordinance Rooms
Four ordinance rooms, eleven sealing rooms, one baptistry, and a celestial room.

First Temple President
Marriner Wood Merrill, 1884–1906. Twenty-two years, still the longest tenure in the temple's history.

Construction Story
  • Built largely by volunteer labor. More than $600,000 in time, goods, and cash was donated, and more than 25,000 people worked on the building over seven years.
  • Brigham Young died three months after the groundbreaking. John Taylor, who succeeded him, dedicated the finished building seven years later.
  • Primary children in the Cache Valley Stake raised about $2,300 in a "nickel drive" for building materials. A guard keeping children off the scaffolding was once talked down by a boy who argued that he had paid his nickel and had a right to see the work. The boy got to stand on the scaffolding.
  • Among the volunteers were Sagwitch and roughly 200 Shoshone Saints who had joined the Church eleven years earlier, after surviving the massacre of their people by the United States Army at Bear River. Settled at Washakie on the northern Utah border, the men traveled to Logan in their spare time to haul stone and prepare plaster, donating thousands of hours. About a year after the dedication, Sagwitch and four others spent four days in the finished temple performing ordinances for family members killed at Bear River.

Symbolism & Design
  • The castellated form, with battlements, squared towers, and a fortress silhouette, is the visual signature Logan shares with Manti and with almost nothing else in the temple system.
  • The exterior was originally painted a pinkish off-white to conceal the dark, rough-hewn limestone underneath. The paint was allowed to weather away in the early 1900s, and the exposed stone became the building's defining feature.
  • Rows of arched windows in white frames run the length of both long elevations.

Changes Over Time
  • December 4, 1917: fire broke out on the temple's east side, traced to faulty wiring in a switchboard inside a closet beneath the main stairway. It damaged walls, carpet, furniture, windows, and paintings. Members repaired it in about three months.
  • 1976: closed for a complete interior reconstruction. The interior was gutted and the roof removed, leaving only the exterior walls and interior floors. The hand-painted murals and pioneer craftsmanship were lost, and the progressive muraled rooms were replaced with stationary rooms equipped for film. President Kimball, who rededicated the building, regretted the loss.
  • 1979: reopened after a public open house that drew 213,184 guests against an expected 90,000. There were 19,205 on the busiest day, with the line stretching seven blocks.
  • 2009: grounds renovated. A 1970s water feature gave way to an oval reflecting pool, and heated sidewalks were added for Cache Valley snow.
  • April 2019: President Nelson announced that Logan, among other pioneer-era temples, would be renovated. Plans have not been released.

Trivia
  • Between the 1884 dedication and the 1976 closure, 26,258,390 ordinances were performed here, more than 18 percent of all temple work in the Church at that time.
  • The first temple built with progressive muraled ordinance rooms for a live-acted endowment presentation.
  • One sitting and four future Presidents of the Church spoke at the 1979 rededication: Spencer W. Kimball, Ezra Taft Benson, Howard W. Hunter, Gordon B. Hinckley, and Thomas S. Monson.
  • In 1897 a two-story stone barn was built a block east to stable the animals of traveling patrons. Automobiles made it obsolete by the 1910s. It was placed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1985 and still stands at 368 East 200 North.

Provo Utah Temple (1972–2024)

Status
This building no longer stands. It closed on February 24, 2024, and was taken down rather than renovated. A replacement, the Provo Utah Rock Canyon Temple, is under construction on the same hill, set west of the original foundation where the slope is flatter. Everything below describes the 1972 building.

Location
Provo, Utah. A 17-acre site on the east bench at the mouth of Rock Canyon, overlooking the city, Utah Lake, and the length of Utah Valley. Brigham Young University bordered the grounds to the southwest, and the Provo Missionary Training Center stood across the street.

Temple Number
The 15th dedicated temple in operation. It was the sixth temple built in Utah and the first in Utah County.

Announced
August 14, 1967, by Hugh B. Brown and N. Eldon Tanner of the First Presidency, in a meeting with 28 local stake presidencies. It was the first Utah temple announced after the Salt Lake Temple was dedicated in 1893, a gap of nearly 75 years.

Groundbreaking
September 15, 1969. Hugh B. Brown broke ground and Joseph Fielding Smith dedicated the site the same day. The cornerstone was set on May 21, 1971, while the building was still going up.

Dedicated
February 9, 1972, by Joseph Fielding Smith, in two sessions. President Smith presided but asked Harold B. Lee to read the prayer he had written. More than 70,000 people attended, because the sessions were carried by closed-circuit television to the Marriott Center and four other venues on the BYU campus.

Architecture
Emil B. Fetzer, Church architect. Modern and functional. White cast stone with gold anodized aluminum grilles and bronze glass panels, set as a flat round base with a single spire rising from the center. 130,825 square feet across four floors, standing 175 feet high, of which the spire accounted for 118 feet.

Ordinance Rooms
Six ordinance rooms, arranged so a new session could begin every 20 minutes, along with a celestial room, twelve sealing rooms, and a baptistry on the below-ground floor.

First Temple President
Harold Glen Clark, 1972 to 1976, with Mary Deane Peterson Gilbert Clark as matron.

Construction Story
  • The decision came out of arithmetic. By the mid-1960s roughly 52 percent of all ordinance work in the Church was being performed in three buildings: Logan, Manti, and Salt Lake. Temples for Provo and Ogden were announced in 1967 to take the load off them.
  • Fetzer designed both under a single basic plan, with efficiency, convenience, and economical construction as the stated priorities. The two buildings went up at the same time and were nearly identical until Ogden was given a new exterior in the early 2010s.
  • Provo's groundbreaking came one week after Ogden's, the first time two temple groundbreakings were held in the same month.
  • Several thousand people turned out on May 21, 1971, for the cornerstone ceremony, with the walls and spire already standing.

Symbolism & Design
  • Circulation drove the plan. Six ordinance rooms ringed a celestial room at the center of the top floor, and a corridor ran the full circle of the top two levels. Fetzer took the loop from a park in Copenhagen encircled by an elliptical roadway. Patrons moved through without crossing paths, and Church News noted it was almost impossible to get lost inside.
  • The original design called for a gold-leafed angel Moroni on the gold spire. The statue was dropped before the building was finished.
  • Many members read the white base as the pillar of cloud and the gold spire as the pillar of fire from Exodus. That reading did not come from the design team. Fred Baker, who worked closely with Fetzer, said flatly that "we didn't have any symbolism in mind" and that the work was focused on what happened inside the building. Church News published a correction to that effect in 2024, citing Richard Cowan.

Changes Over Time
  • The building opened as simply the Provo Temple. It became the Provo Utah Temple in 1999, when the Church revised its temple naming convention.
  • In May 2003, 31 years after dedication, an angel Moroni statue was placed on the spire and the spire was repainted from gold to white. That is the version most people photographed.
  • In the October 2021 general conference, Russell M. Nelson announced the reconstruction of the temple following the dedication of the Orem Utah Temple. An exterior rendering of the redesign was released in November 2021, and the closure date was announced in June 2023.
  • On February 20, 2024, the First Presidency announced that the rebuilt temple would carry a new name, the Provo Utah Rock Canyon Temple. The original closed four days later and demolition followed.

Trivia
  • For decades this was the busiest temple in the Church. In 1973, its first full year of operation, 17.7 percent of all ordinances performed worldwide were performed here.
  • Richard Cowan and Justin Bray called it the "working temple." It ran as many as 50 endowment sessions a day, the first starting at 5:30 a.m. and the last ending near 11:00 p.m. In 1976 it set a record with 76,000 endowments completed in a single month.
  • The public open house ran January 8 to 29, 1972, and drew 246,201 visitors. Special tours were arranged for groups with particular needs, including one for visually impaired guests, whom the temple president led through while describing the building aloud.
  • Sessions in Spanish and sessions for patrons who were hearing impaired both began in 1974. Portuguese, German, Japanese, Mandarin, and others followed, and by 2022 ordinances could be received here in 82 languages.

Taylorsville Utah Temple

Location
Taylorsville, Utah. A 7.5-acre site at 2603 West 4700 South, on the west side of the Salt Lake Valley at the southwest corner of the Interstate 215 interchange. A Church meetinghouse and a recreational field stood there before.

Temple Number
The 192nd dedicated temple in operation. It was the twenty-first temple built in Utah and the fifth in the Salt Lake Valley, after Salt Lake in 1893, Jordan River in 1981, and Draper and Oquirrh Mountain in 2009.

Announced
October 5, 2019, by Russell M. Nelson during the women's session of general conference. The site was identified about ten weeks later, on December 11, 2019.

Groundbreaking
October 31, 2020, presided over by Gerrit W. Gong of the Quorum of the Twelve. Local COVID-19 restrictions kept it to a small gathering of Church and community leaders.

Dedicated
June 2, 2024, by Gerrit W. Gong, in two sessions broadcast to every congregation in the temple district.

Architecture
Structural steel with stone cladding, in a style the Church calls pioneer-era Gothic. Three stories, 73,492 square feet, with a single attached octagonal tower.

Ordinance Rooms
Four instruction rooms, four sealing rooms, and one baptistry.

Construction Story
  • The site came with a demolition attached. The meetinghouse that stood there served as the stake center for the Taylorsville Utah Valley Park Stake and had to come down before the temple could go up.
  • The groundbreaking was personal for the presiding officer. Gerrit W. Gong's wife, Susan, is a Taylorsville native, and her father, Richard Lindsay, was the bishop of the congregation that built the meetinghouse the temple replaced.
  • Taylorsville City had no zoning category that fit. On April 1, 2020, the city council passed three ordinances and a resolution, two of which created a new classification, Site Specific Development, Institutional, Temple, and rezoned the property out of Single Family Residential into it.
  • The building grew between rendering and ribbon. The exterior rendering released in August 2020 described roughly 70,000 square feet; the finished temple came in at 73,492.

Symbolism & Design
  • The architect worked from local pioneer tabernacles rather than from other temples. The arches and motifs come out of the tabernacles built in the communities along the Wasatch Front, which is what "pioneer-era Gothic" is pointing at.
  • The flowers in the exterior art glass are stylized versions of three plants that grow in the west valley: bird's-foot trefoil, "Red Beauty" bergenia, and broad-leaved gilia.
  • The deep burgundy, lavender, and gold palette borrows from Gothic architecture but was chosen to sit inside the natural colors of the west side of the valley rather than against them.
  • The quatrefoil runs from the architecture out into the site and back inside again. It sets the paving pattern in the four main plazas and appears again as decorative metalwork along the baptismal font railing.
  • Interior stone is Perlatino from Italy throughout, with Crema Ella in the sealing rooms and celestial room. The art glass and decorative painting inside were designed by FFKR Architects.

Trivia
  • More than 265,000 people toured the temple during the public open house, which ran April 13 to May 18, 2024, excluding Sundays.
  • When the site was announced, Church leaders said one reason for it was that a temple at that interchange would be a landmark for motorists on the beltway.
  • The site is tight enough that nearly half the landscaping sits on top of structure rather than on ground. That meant limited soil depth and sub-grade anchors for the tree rootballs, along with drought-tolerant planting, minimal turf, and smart-controlled drip irrigation.
  • At the dedication, Gong named the communities the district draws from, among them Bennion, Kearns, Magna, Midvale, Murray, Granger, Hunter, and Taylorsville, and said of them: "Many have deep roots, many are new, all are pioneers."

Boise Idaho Temple

Location
Boise, Idaho. The temple stands at 1211 South Cole Road on a 4.83-acre site beside Interstate 84 at the Cole Road exit, at an elevation of 2,754 feet, where its white granite and six spires make it a landmark for freeway travelers.

Temple Number
The 27th dedicated temple of the Church, and the second built in Idaho, following the Idaho Falls Idaho Temple (1945).

Announced
March 31, 1982, by President Gordon B. Hinckley, then a counselor in the First Presidency. Ground was broken before the year was out.

Groundbreaking
December 18, 1982. Elder Mark E. Petersen of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles presided and dedicated the site; about 5,000 members gathered on the site in the December cold to watch.

Dedicated
May 25 through 30, 1984, by President Gordon B. Hinckley, then second counselor in the First Presidency, in 24 sessions. About 29,000 people attended.

Rededicated
Twice: February 14, 1987, by Elder James E. Faust, after an addition; and November 18, 2012, by President Thomas S. Monson, in three sessions, after a 15-month renovation.

Architecture
Designed by the Church architectural staff with Ron Thurber & Associates of Boise, a modern adaptation of the six-spire design. The exterior is temple white granite quarried in China, beneath a broad sloping roof and six detached spires. The temple encloses 35,868 square feet and rises 112 feet to the angel Moroni statue on the east tower.

Ordinance Rooms
Four instruction rooms, three sealing rooms, and a baptistry.

First Temple President
Seth D. Redford, 1984 to 1987.

Construction Story
  • In 1939, a group of prominent Boise businessmen offered President Heber J. Grant any available site in the city, hoping Idaho's first temple would rise in the capital. Idaho Falls was chosen instead, and President Grant told the group that a temple would come to Boise when membership there increased.
  • Organizers expected about 70,000 visitors at the public open house, held May 1 through 19, 1984. They got 128,716.
  • Convert baptisms in the area more than doubled in the month after the open house, and people called the mission office asking how they could be baptized.
  • The 24 dedicatory sessions were, at the time, the most held for any temple since the Salt Lake Temple in 1893.

Symbolism & Design
  • The six detached spires made Boise the first six-spire temple built since the Washington D.C. Temple in 1974, and before that the Salt Lake Temple in 1893.
  • Syringa, Idaho's state flower, appears throughout the interior in art glass and decorative painting, set against blues, greens, and earth tones. The art glass is the work of Holdman Studios, with murals by Dale Jolley.
  • Glass from the temple's original windows was crushed and worked into the new art glass installed during the 2012 renovation, so the first building's windows survive inside the current ones.

Changes Over Time
  • Heavy use forced an expansion just two and a half years after dedication. Elder James E. Faust rededicated the enlarged temple on February 14, 1987; the addition brought a new baptistry, additional offices, and expanded patron facilities.
  • The temple closed on July 11, 2011, for a 15-month renovation led by CTA Architects Engineers of Boise, with structural reinforcement, an expanded basement, and new grounds featuring a stone-encased reflecting pool. The original marble tile exterior was replaced with temple white granite after the adhesive behind the tile began to seep through and discolor the walls.
  • A new gold-leafed angel Moroni was set atop the east spire on February 16, 2012, and the cornerstone, which had been inside the building since the 1987 expansion, was moved to the exterior northeast corner on August 29, 2012.
  • Nearly 170,000 people toured the renovated temple during the fall 2012 open house. The night before the rededication, 9,200 youth performed a cultural celebration titled "Treasure the Light," with 4,000 dancers, 99 fiddlers, and a choir of more than 1,000 voices.

Trivia
  • Boise is a sister building to the Dallas Texas and Chicago Illinois temples, and its efficiency-driven design was adapted for 14 other temples built between 1984 and 1989.
  • Before the 1984 open house, Idaho Governor John Evans, Lieutenant Governor David Leroy, and Secretary of State Pete Cenarusa toured the temple in a special preview, along with 246 ministers of other faiths and their family members.
  • At its 2012 rededication, the temple served about 100,000 members in 31 stakes across western Idaho and eastern Oregon.

Temple facts verified as of August 25, 2026.

Bountiful Utah Temple

Location
Bountiful, Utah. The temple stands at 640 South Bountiful Boulevard, in the foothills of the east bench overlooking the Great Salt Lake, about nine miles north of Salt Lake City, at an elevation of 5,160 feet.

Temple Number
The 47th operating temple of the Church, the eighth in Utah, and the first in Davis County.

Announced
February 2, 1990, by a First Presidency letter to local leaders in Davis County: "We have now determined to undertake the construction of a temple on this site." The Church had announced the purchase of the hillside property for a possible temple on May 28, 1988.

Groundbreaking
May 2, 1992. President Ezra Taft Benson presided, with his counselors President Gordon B. Hinckley and President Thomas S. Monson participating. About 7,500 people attended on the site and 2,500 more watched by video.

Dedicated
January 8 through 14, 1995, by President Howard W. Hunter, in 28 sessions. President Hunter attended six of the sessions and spoke in four; Apostles read his dedicatory prayer in the remainder.

Architecture
A modern single-spire design by architect of record Allen B. Erekson, with Keith Stepan as project architect. The exterior is Bethel white granite quarried near Sharon, Vermont. The temple encloses 104,000 square feet and rises 176 feet to the angel Moroni statue atop its spire.

Ordinance Rooms
Four instruction rooms, eight sealing rooms, and a baptistry.

First Temple President
Harold C. Yancey, 1994 to 1997.

Construction Story
  • The groundbreaking crowd was so large that President Hinckley compared it to "the days of King Benjamin," when the people gathered around the temple by families.
  • Architect Allen B. Erekson stated the design goal plainly: "What we are trying to accomplish in the Bountiful Utah Temple is to have a level of elegance that doesn't distract from the Spirit."
  • During the public open house, November 5 through December 17, 1994, exactly 870,361 visitors toured the temple, assisted by some 45,000 volunteers.

Symbolism & Design
  • Exterior detailing represents the sun, moon, and stars, a reference to the scriptural descriptions of the three degrees of glory.
  • The art glass, created by Arthur Stern Studio of Oakland, California, carries a Jacob's Ladder motif of ascending detail, with beveled crystal that refracts sunlight into rainbow effects inside.
  • Interior colors deepen and lighten by floor: rich, warm tones on the lower levels give way to lighter, more elegant tones as one ascends.

Changes Over Time
  • Lightning struck the angel Moroni statue on May 22, 2016, and a replacement statue was set atop the spire on June 1, 2016.

Trivia
  • The 28 dedicatory sessions drew 201,655 attendees, reported as the largest attendance at any temple dedication in the history of the Church.
  • Bountiful was one of only two temples dedicated by President Howard W. Hunter, whose presidency lasted nine months; he died less than two months after the dedication.
  • The temple's floor plan was adapted for the Mount Timpanogos Utah Temple, dedicated the following year.

Temple facts verified as of August 19, 2026.

Albuquerque New Mexico Temple

Location
Albuquerque, New Mexico. An 8.5-acre site at 10301 San Francisco Road NE, on the northeast heights of the city at an elevation of 5,729 feet, with the Sandia Mountains rising directly to the east.

Temple Number
The 73rd dedicated temple in operation, and the first built in New Mexico.

Announced
April 4, 1997, by Gordon B. Hinckley.

Groundbreaking
June 20, 1998, presided over by Lynn A. Mickelsen of the Seventy, then president of the North America Southwest Area.

Dedicated
March 5, 2000, by Gordon B. Hinckley, in four sessions attended by more than 13,500 Latter-day Saints.

Architecture
Fanning Bard Tatum Architects of Albuquerque. Desert Rose precast concrete with Texas Pearl granite at the base, 34,245 square feet, with a single attached end spire carrying the angel Moroni.

Ordinance Rooms
Two instruction rooms, three sealing rooms, and one baptistry.

Construction Story
  • The public open house ran February 17 to February 26, 2000, nine days, and drew roughly 70,000 visitors.
  • The mountains the temple was sited against turned out to have an opinion about the front door. The original hinged entrance doors were replaced with glass sliding doors because of the winds coming off the Sandias.

Symbolism & Design
  • The exterior was chosen to answer the landscape rather than stand apart from it. The Desert Rose concrete and Texas Pearl granite read pink in the evening light, which is exactly what the Sandia range does at sunset, a color the mountains are named for.
  • Church News described the building as the first of its design in the Church, and framed the temple as a meeting point for a region where three cultures come together: American Indian, Hispanic and Anglo.

Changes Over Time
  • A 2019 renovation converted the original kitchen and cafeteria into office space, a change made across many temples of this era as patron meal service was discontinued.

Trivia
  • The temple stands at 5,729 feet above sea level, on the high desert bench that runs up toward the mountains from the Rio Grande.
  • It arrived in a crowded season. The Church's May 2000 conference report covered seven temple dedications in a single article, Albuquerque among them.

Billings Montana Temple

Billings, Montana. A 10-acre site at 3100 Rim Point Drive, on the rimrocks on the west side of the city, above the Yellowstone Valley.

Temple Number
The 66th dedicated temple in operation, and the first built in Montana.

Announced
August 16, 1996, by Gordon B. Hinckley.

Groundbreaking
March 28, 1998, presided over by Hugh W. Pinnock of the Seventy, then president of the North America Central Area.

November 20 and 21, 1999, by Gordon B. Hinckley, in eight sessions attended by more than 12,000 members.

Architecture
Wyoming white dolomite precast concrete, 33,800 square feet, with a single central spire carrying the angel Moroni.

Two instruction rooms, arranged for two-stage progressive sessions, three sealing rooms, and one baptistry.

Brigham City Utah Temple

Location
Brigham City, Utah. A 3.1 acre site on downtown Main Street, directly across the street from the historic Box Elder Stake Tabernacle.

Temple Number
The 139th dedicated temple of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, the 14th in Utah, and the first in Box Elder County.

Announced
October 3, 2009, by President Thomas S. Monson at the 179th Semiannual General Conference, one of five temples announced that morning.

Groundbreaking
July 31, 2010. President Boyd K. Packer, president of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles and a Brigham City native, presided.

Dedicated
September 23, 2012, by President Boyd K. Packer, in three sessions.

Architecture
FFKR Architects, with Big-D Construction as general contractor. The design deliberately echoes Utah's pioneer-era temples. Warm white precast concrete exterior, 36,000 square feet, twin end spires and an angel Moroni statue, rising 165 feet.

Ordinance Rooms
Two instruction rooms in a two-stage progressive arrangement, three sealing rooms, and a baptistry whose font rests on twelve cast bronze oxen.

First Temple President
Preston J. Checketts, with Louise B. Checketts as matron, 2012 to 2015.

Construction Story
  • The temple stands on the site of the old Central School, a three-story elementary school built in 1901 and rebuilt after a 1947 fire. Boyd K. Packer attended grade school there as a boy; six decades later he returned to break ground for a temple on the same spot, then dedicated it in his hometown.
  • The angel Moroni statue was set in place on July 12, 2011, more than a year before the building was finished.
  • The public open house ran from August 18 to September 15, 2012, and drew nearly 404,500 visitors. The busiest single day was Labor Day, when 25,000 people walked through.

Symbolism & Design
  • Peach blossoms run through the whole building: in the art glass of the second-floor windows, in the furniture, and in the hand-carved carpet of the celestial room. Elder William R. Walker explained during the 2012 open house that the motif carries no religious significance; it is a tribute to the area's fruit-growing heritage.
  • Twenty-six fruit trees were planted on the temple grounds, continuing the same nod to the region's orchards.
  • The exterior deliberately recalls the Church's pioneer-era temples such as Salt Lake and Manti. Elder Walker put it simply: "It looks like a historic temple."
  • The sealing waiting room displays portraits of Brigham Young, the city's namesake, and Lorenzo Snow, who served as stake president there.

Trivia
  • Brigham City was one of five temples announced in a single conference session, alongside Concepción Chile, Fortaleza Brazil, Fort Lauderdale Florida, and Sapporo Japan.
  • In that announcement, President Monson noted that 83 percent of Church members lived within 200 miles of a temple.
  • At its dedication the temple served about 40,000 Latter-day Saints in 13 stakes across northern Utah and southeastern Idaho.

Burley Idaho Temple

Location
Burley, Idaho. A 10.12-acre site at 40 South 150 East, in the Magic Valley farming country of south central Idaho.

Temple Number
The 212th dedicated temple in operation, and the seventh dedicated in Idaho.

Announced
April 4, 2021, by Russell M. Nelson at the close of the 191st Annual General Conference.

Groundbreaking
June 4, 2022, presided over by Brent H. Nielson of the Presidency of the Seventy.

Dedicated
January 11, 2026, by Dallin H. Oaks. It was the first temple he dedicated as President of the Church, and the first dedication of 2026.

Architecture
Naylor Wentworth Lund Architects. A two-story steel frame clad in Bianco Sardo granite, fabricated in Millcreek, Utah. 45,300 square feet, 172 feet to the top of a single attached end spire.

Ordinance Rooms
Four instruction rooms, three sealing rooms, and one baptistry.

Construction Story
  • The ground it stands on was given. Leroy Funk and his siblings donated farmland their family had worked for decades. Funk put the credit elsewhere: "It is here because of the faithful ones who came before."
  • Latter-day Saints have been in the Burley area since 1879. The first branch, fourteen members, was organized in a log cabin in May 1880.
  • The public open house ran November 6 to November 22, 2025, through a stretch of unseasonably warm and sunny weather that had the tour coordinators joking about handing out sunscreen in November.

Symbolism & Design
  • The art glass is drawn from the crop the valley is known for. Its patterns are the blossoms and leaves of the potato plant, with the sugar beet fields of the Magic Valley informing the wider design.
  • The color palette was taken from the farmland and the open sky above it: blue, gold, amber, cream, orange, peach and green.
  • Interior stonework is Botticino Classico marble with Jerusalem Gold and Verde Guatemala accents, and the artwork inside was commissioned around the local landscape and the early Latter-day Saints of Burley.

Trivia
  • President Oaks chose Burley for his first dedication as President of the Church because of where he grew up. He lived in nearby Twin Falls as a boy for about five years, and said the place was "close to my heart."
  • The drive to the temple went from about 45 minutes to about five. Before Burley, members here attended the Twin Falls Idaho Temple.
  • Susan Young, Twin Falls temple matron from 2016 to 2019, remembered Burley youth arriving for baptisms at 3:30 in the morning, week after week. The baptistry would be full of young people sitting in white, and quiet enough to hear a pin drop.
  • The open house was run to be reachable: 143 tours in Spanish, nine in American Sign Language, and one tactile tour for visitors who needed it.

Cody Wyoming Temple

Status
Under construction. The public open house runs August 27 through September 12, 2026, excluding Sundays, and admission is free with no reservation required. Dedication is scheduled for Sunday, October 25, 2026.

Location
555 Temple View Lane, Cody, Wyoming. A 4.69-acre site northwest of Skyline Drive at Cody Canal, in the northwestern corner of the state near the Montana border, at an elevation of 5,134 feet with Heart Mountain on the horizon.

Temple Number
The third temple built in Wyoming, following Star Valley in 2016 and Casper in 2024. Its number among dedicated temples will be fixed at dedication.

Announced
October 3, 2021, by President Russell M. Nelson, at the October 2021 general conference, among thirteen temples announced that session.

Groundbreaking
September 27, 2024. Elder Steven R. Bangerter, First Counselor in the North America Central Area Presidency, presided and offered the site dedicatory prayer. Elder Kevin R. Duncan, Executive Director of the Temple Department, also attended.

Architecture
A single-story building of 9,950 square feet, 101 feet to the top of the spire. The exterior is precast concrete panels. A single attached central tower rises as a multi-tiered steeple capped with a gold pyramidal spire. The official exterior rendering was released March 27, 2023.

Ordinance Rooms
One instruction room, one sealing room, and one baptistry.

Construction Story
  • The site was announced in March 2023 as an empty field northwest of Skyline Drive, roughly seventeen months after the temple itself was announced.
  • Modular construction methods carried the project at unusual speed, with the exterior essentially finished about eighteen months after work began.
  • In his site dedicatory prayer, Elder Bangerter asked a blessing on the surrounding community rather than only on the Church membership, praying that neighbors would feel a spirit of peace and that the temple's presence would bring added joy, prosperity, beauty, and unity to their lives.

Symbolism & Design
  • The gold pyramidal spire replaces the angel Moroni statue found on many older temples, a choice increasingly common among the small single-story temples built in this era.
  • At 9,950 square feet, Cody is built to the scale of its community rather than to the scale of a regional temple. The single instruction room and single sealing room are the design's honest statement about who it is for.

Trivia
  • Nearly 67,000 Latter-day Saints live in Wyoming, meeting in more than 170 congregations, roughly one in every nine residents of the state.
  • Members in northwest Wyoming currently travel to the Billings Montana Temple. Cody will end that drive for them.
  • Cody is already home to the Historic Cody Mural and Museum, a Church meetinghouse whose domed ceiling carries a large mural depicting the Restoration and the westward migration. The chapel and visitors' center are open to the public during summer months.
  • Wyoming's pioneer connection is not incidental. Latter-day Saint companies crossed the state throughout the 1840s to 1860s on their way to the Salt Lake Valley.

April 7, 2019, by President Russell M. Nelson, at general conference.

Draper, Utah, on a hillside at the south end of the Salt Lake Valley, below Corner Canyon.

Ephraim Utah Temple

Status
Under construction. The public open house runs September 2 through September 19, 2026, excluding Sundays, following a media day on August 31. Elder Ronald A. Rasband of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles is scheduled to dedicate the temple on October 11, 2026, in a single 10:00 a.m. session broadcast to all units in the temple district.

Location
Ephraim, Utah. The temple stands on a 9.16-acre site at 400 East and 200 North, at an elevation of 5,567 feet in the Sanpete Valley. Ephraim is Sanpete County's largest population center and the home of Snow College.

Temple Number
The second temple in Sanpete County, following the Manti Utah Temple, dedicated in 1888. Its number among the Church's dedicated temples will be fixed at its dedication.

Announced
May 1, 2021, by President Russell M. Nelson in a prerecorded message shown at a press conference inside the Manti Tabernacle, the same event at which the Church announced revised renovation plans for the Manti Utah Temple.

Groundbreaking
August 27, 2022. President Russell M. Nelson presided, accompanied by Sister Wendy Nelson, Elder Walter F. González, and Elder Kevin R. Duncan. Utah Governor Spencer J. Cox and other government leaders participated.

Architecture
A three-story temple of approximately 39,000 square feet. The exterior features large arched windows and an arched entry, with a multilevel octagonal tower topped by a domed cupola.

Ordinance Rooms
Four instruction rooms seating 30 each, three sealing rooms, and a baptistry.

Construction Story
  • The temple began with a change of plans seven miles away. President Nelson said that shortly after the April 2021 general conference he received "very clear instruction" that the pioneer craftsmanship of the Manti Utah Temple should be preserved rather than replaced in renovation, and that a new temple should be built in Ephraim to serve the area alongside it.
  • President Nelson presided at the groundbreaking in person as an unannounced guest. "We are deeply grateful for our ancestors," he said at the site. "They have laid a foundation of faith that undergirds our spiritual strength."
  • The prophet's own family is part of that foundation. "My dear mother was born in Ephraim, not far from this very temple site. My father was born in Manti," he said at the groundbreaking. Three of his four grandparents were born in Ephraim, and all eight of his great-grandparents lived there, converts to the Church from England, Denmark, Norway, and Sweden.

Symbolism & Design
  • The central octagonal tower carries four arched windows at its base and eight on the tower itself, echoing the arched windows that wrap the body of the building.

Trivia
  • Latter-day Saint settlers first entered the Sanpete Valley in the fall of 1849, and Ephraim was settled in 1854, primarily by Scandinavian immigrant converts. The valley's first stake was organized in 1877.
  • The temple shares its scheduled dedication day, October 11, 2026, with the Miraflores Guatemala City Guatemala Temple.

Heber Valley Utah Temple

Status
Under construction. Site work began in August 2025, nearly three years after groundbreaking, and crews were pouring the temple's deep foundation slab in August 2026. Dates for the public open house and dedication have not yet been announced.

Location
Heber City, Utah. The temple is rising on a 17.9-acre site southeast of 1400 East Center Street, at an elevation of 5,711 feet in the Heber Valley, a mountain valley about 40 miles from Salt Lake City.

Temple Number
The first temple built in Wasatch County and the 28th announced for Utah. Its number among the Church's dedicated temples will be fixed at its dedication.

Announced
October 3, 2021, by President Russell M. Nelson during the 191st Semiannual General Conference, one of 13 temples announced at the close of the Sunday afternoon session.

Groundbreaking
October 8, 2022. President Russell M. Nelson presided and offered the site dedicatory prayer before a crowd of more than 600. Elder Kevin R. Duncan, General Authority Seventy and executive director of the Temple Department, also spoke.

Architecture
A three-story temple of approximately 88,000 square feet, with rows of arched windows, two attached end towers topped by domed cupolas, and a planned height of 210 feet.

Ordinance Rooms
Four instruction rooms and four sealing rooms.

Construction Story
  • The Church had announced that Elder Kevin R. Duncan would preside at the groundbreaking. Instead, President Nelson made a surprise appearance and presided himself, telling the crowd, "Today, we will begin the work by breaking ground for a temple in this unique and wonderful valley."
  • The temple will stand on land purchased in 1946 by George Holmes Sr., a World War II veteran and the son of immigrant parents, and his wife Clara. President Nelson said of him, "For years, he had dreamt of building a forever home with his beloved Clara. In a very real way, his dream will be realized."
  • Wasatch County approved the temple in November 2023 through a legislative development agreement, and a group of residents sued the county three weeks later. Although a building permit had been issued, the Church voluntarily waited to build while the case was reviewed; a district judge upheld the county's approval on July 23, 2025, and site work began the following month.
  • Construction paused again in September 2025 when the Utah Supreme Court agreed to hear the residents' appeal, then resumed in February 2026 after the court unanimously lifted the injunction, allowing work to continue while the appeal is decided.
  • The site sits on shallow groundwater. Before foundation work, the Utah Division of Water Rights approved 20 dewatering wells; a 2023 study estimated up to a million gallons a day would need to be pumped, settled in tanks, and discharged into adjacent Lake Creek.

Symbolism & Design
  • The design defers to the valley's dark skies. The Church dropped the wall-wash floodlighting typical of temple exteriors, warmed the lighting from 4000 to 3000 Kelvin, adjusted the color and texture of the exterior stone to reduce reflected light, and committed to shutting off all outdoor lighting at 11 each night. Principal architect Curtis Miner told the county council it "will be one of the dimmest temples in the world."

Trivia
  • Heber City is named for Heber C. Kimball, the apostle whose missionary service in England in the 1840s converted many of the families who settled the valley. Heber's first ward was organized in 1860.
  • As President and Sister Nelson left the groundbreaking, the crowd broke into "We Thank Thee, O God, for a Prophet."

Temple facts verified as of August 25, 2026.

South Jordan, Utah. The temple takes its name from the Jordan River, which runs through the valley below it, rather than from the city it stands in. The site was donated to the Church.

Temple Number
The 20th dedicated temple.

Announced
February 3, 1978, by President Spencer W. Kimball.

Groundbreaking
June 9, 1979. President Spencer W. Kimball presided, before a crowd of about 10,000.

Dedicated
November 16 to 20, 1981, by President Marion G. Romney of the First Presidency, in 15 sessions.

Rededicated
May 20, 2018, by President Henry B. Eyring, following a two year renovation.

Architecture
Cast stone set with white marble chips. The tower looks like the same material but is built of cemlite, a fiberglass product chosen to reduce weight. 148,236 square feet, rising 219 feet to a single attached central spire with an angel Moroni statue.

Ordinance Rooms
Six instruction rooms, sixteen sealing rooms, one baptistry.

Construction Story
  • This was the first temple of the modern era built entirely with donated funds. By the May 1979 deadline, members of the district had raised 110 percent of the amount needed, and had done it ahead of schedule.
  • Rather than turn the first earth with a ceremonial shovel, President Kimball put on a hard hat, climbed onto a front end loader and scooped it himself, in keeping with his counsel to lengthen our stride.
  • The ground the temple stands on was given to the Church rather than purchased.

Symbolism & Design
  • The exterior is cast stone studded with white marble chips, which catches light across the face of the building.

  • The temple closed in 2016 for a full renovation, which brought seismic upgrades, modernized mechanical and electrical systems and a redesigned interior.
