Kirtland Temple

Location
Kirtland, Ohio, at 9020 Chillicothe Road. The building stands on a bluff about 25 miles east of Cleveland, overlooking the Chagrin Valley.

Status
Not an operating temple. It is preserved as a historic site and open to visitors of any faith at no charge, with guided tours beginning at the adjacent visitors' center. No ordinances are performed there, so it has no temple number, no temple district, and no temple president.

Announced
December 27, 1832. A revelation recorded that day, now Doctrine and Covenants 88, directed the Saints in Kirtland to establish a house of prayer, fasting, faith, learning, glory, order, and God.

Construction Begun
June 5, 1833. The cornerstones were laid on July 23, 1833.

Dedicated
March 27, 1836, by Joseph Smith. The service was repeated several days later for those who could not be seated the first time.

Architecture
No professional architect. The First Presidency of the day, Joseph Smith, Sidney Rigdon, and Frederick G. Williams, reported receiving the design by vision in 1833, and the plan called for an interior 55 feet wide by 65 feet long. The walls are locally quarried sandstone laid as rubble masonry, finished in stucco and scored to imitate cut coursed stone. Roughly 15,000 square feet across three levels. The exterior follows the New England Protestant meetinghouse form with Federal and Gothic elements: lancet windows along the sides, ten small dormers lighting the attic story, and a bell tower over the front.

Construction Story
  • The walls were supposed to be brick. Frederick G. Williams supervised brick production from April to September 1833, but the crews had no experience and the bricks were unusable. The effort was abandoned by mid-September, leaving a finished stone foundation with nothing to build on top of it.
  • The fix came from Artemus Millet, a Canadian convert with experience on mills, chimneys, and foundations, who reached Kirtland in late October 1833. Noting how much sandstone the local quarries held, he proposed rubble masonry walls under a stucco finish, which is how the temple was actually built. Most retellings credit Brigham Young with recruiting him. Millet's own reminiscence and Hyrum Smith's papers say the written request came from Hyrum.
  • Zion's Camp emptied the site in the summer of 1834. Heber C. Kimball later recalled that only ten or fifteen men were left in Kirtland, and that at times no more than five or six were working on the building.
  • When the design was presented in June 1833, Hyrum Smith ran home for a scythe to start clearing the wheat field on the building site. Asked by his mother where he was going with it, he said he was "determined to be the first at the work."
  • What the temple cost was never settled. Ira Ames took over the building committee's books and found them in disorder. Scholarly estimates range from $30,000 to $100,000, with a figure near $40,000 the most commonly cited.

Historical Significance
  • This was the first temple the Latter Day Saints completed. Its formal name was the House of the Lord. The word temple was not yet in general use, and Joseph Smith's records also refer to the building as the Chapel.
  • The dedication set a pattern later dedications still follow. Joseph Smith read a prayer he had received by revelation, now Doctrine and Covenants 109, the congregation gave the Hosanna Shout, and they sang "The Spirit of God," which William W. Phelps wrote for the occasion. All three became standard elements of temple dedications afterward.
  • On April 3, 1836, one week after the dedication, Joseph Smith and Oliver Cowdery recorded a vision at the pulpits in which Moses, Elias, and Elijah conferred priesthood keys. The account is published as Doctrine and Covenants 110, and Latter-day Saints trace the authority for temple sealings and family history work to it.
  • The building functioned as a school as much as a meetinghouse. As many as 140 people studied reading, writing, history, geography, and Hebrew grammar in the third-floor rooms during the week.

Ownership History
  • A financial crisis struck Kirtland a year after the dedication. A dissenting faction led by Warren Parrish tried to seize the building, an unknown arsonist later tried to burn it, and most of the Saints left Ohio for Missouri in 1837 and 1838.
  • In 1880 an Ohio court recognized the heirs of Joseph Smith as holding title. About two decades later the Reorganized Church of Jesus Christ of Latter Day Saints, now Community of Christ, secured ownership through a legal claim of continuous use, and cared for the building from then until 2024.
  • On March 5, 2024, ownership transferred to The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. Discussions had begun in June 2021. The agreement totaled $192.5 million and covered the temple along with historic buildings in Nauvoo, manuscripts, and artifacts, with no value assigned to any single item. Community of Christ stated the proceeds would fund its mission priorities worldwide. The building closed for twenty days and reopened for free public tours on March 25, 2024.

Changes Over Time
  • After the Saints left, the temple served as a venue for private worship and public functions, and was leased for many years as a public school.
  • Community of Christ's predecessor restored the building as closely as possible to its original condition after establishing ownership.
  • The Historic American Buildings Survey documented the temple and its interior plan in 1934. It was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1969 and designated a National Historic Landmark in December 1976.

Trivia
  • The gilt inscription across the front reads House of the Lord, Built by the Church of Christ, 1834, dated two years before the building was finished.
  • The exterior stucco has crushed crockery, china, and glass mixed into it, which makes the walls catch the light. Children gathered the discarded shards. The often repeated story that the women of Kirtland deliberately broke their good china for the purpose has no known historical account behind it.
  • Both main halls carry two sets of tiered pulpits, one at each end, lettered in gilt with initials designating priesthood offices. The pews were built with movable benches so a congregation could face either direction.
  • Truman O. Angell worked here as a carpenter and joiner. He went on to serve as Church architect and to plan the Salt Lake Temple.

Layton, Utah, in Davis County, on the bench between the Wasatch Range and the Great Salt Lake.

Temple Number
The 195th dedicated temple.

Announced
April 1, 2018, by President Russell M. Nelson, in the Sunday afternoon session of general conference.

Groundbreaking
May 23, 2020. Elder Craig C. Christensen, president of the Utah Area, presided, and Elder Randy D. Funk offered the site dedicatory prayer.

Dedicated
June 16, 2024, by Elder David A. Bednar of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles, in two sessions.

Architecture
HNWL Architects of Salt Lake City, with landscape architecture by MGB+A. Precast concrete panels over a structural steel frame and cast in place concrete shear walls. 93,539 square feet, rising 215 feet, with two attached end spires and an angel Moroni statue.

Ordinance Rooms
Four instruction rooms, six sealing rooms, one baptistry.

Construction Story
  • The Church acquired the property on March 30, 2018, two days before the temple was announced.
  • The groundbreaking was held a week early and without advance public notice because of COVID-19 restrictions. A video of the scaled down ceremony was released on May 30, 2020, the date the public event had been scheduled for.
  • The public open house ran April 19 through June 1, 2024, excluding Sundays.

Symbolism & Design
  • The building is styled after Art Nouveau and draws its motifs from Davis County's farming history, when the area was known as the Garden Spot of Utah. Abstracted fruit trees, blossoms, seedlings and leafy branches run through the ornament.
  • The art glass follows that idea in sequence, showing stylized seedlings growing into fruit trees in deep saturated color.
  • A restored Tiffany Studios window titled "The Resurrection," made around 1915, stands at the entrance to the second floor patron waiting area. It was bought from a United Presbyterian church in Amenia, New York, before that building was demolished in 2015.
  • Seven original works of art were commissioned for the building.

  • The Tiffany window is roughly a century older than the building it now hangs in.
  • Layton was dedicated on the same day as the Salta Argentina Temple.

Logan Utah Temple

Location
Logan, Utah. Nine acres occupying an entire city block on an elevated bench of ancient Lake Bonneville, visible for miles across Cache Valley.

Temple Number
The fourth Latter-day Saint temple built, the second still in operation, and the second dedicated in Utah Territory.

Announced
October 6, 1876, by Brigham Young, at the 46th Semiannual General Conference. Young announced a temple for Cache Valley and divided Utah Territory into three temple districts. A letter that December named Logan as the site.

Groundbreaking
May 18, 1877. Elder Orson Pratt dedicated the site; President John W. Young broke ground. Less than a month after ground was broken at Manti, the first time in Church history that two temple groundbreakings fell in the same year.

Dedicated
May 17–19, 1884, by President John Taylor, in three sessions. The only temple John Taylor ever dedicated. Logan officials tidied the city, organized food and lodging for travelers, and ran excursion trains at reduced fare. About 1,500 people attended the first session.

Rededicated
March 13–15, 1979, by President Spencer W. Kimball, in nine sessions.

Architecture
Truman O. Angell, Church architect. Castellated style, shared with the Manti temple. Charles O. Card served as superintendent of construction, John Parry as master mason, William Davis as plastering foreman. The exterior is dark siliceous limestone, with buff-colored limestone reserved for detailed carving because it worked more easily. Five stories, 168 by 224 feet, 86 feet to the roofline. A domed cupola sits above each short end. The east tower rises 170 feet and the west 165, with four octagonal towers at 100 feet each. Originally 59,130 square feet, now 115,507.

Ordinance Rooms
Four ordinance rooms, eleven sealing rooms, one baptistry, and a celestial room.

First Temple President
Marriner Wood Merrill, 1884–1906. Twenty-two years, still the longest tenure in the temple's history.

Construction Story
  • Built largely by volunteer labor. More than $600,000 in time, goods, and cash was donated, and more than 25,000 people worked on the building over seven years.
  • Brigham Young died three months after the groundbreaking. John Taylor, who succeeded him, dedicated the finished building seven years later.
  • Primary children in the Cache Valley Stake raised about $2,300 in a "nickel drive" for building materials. A guard keeping children off the scaffolding was once talked down by a boy who argued that he had paid his nickel and had a right to see the work. The boy got to stand on the scaffolding.
  • Among the volunteers were Sagwitch and roughly 200 Shoshone Saints who had joined the Church eleven years earlier, after surviving the massacre of their people by the United States Army at Bear River. Settled at Washakie on the northern Utah border, the men traveled to Logan in their spare time to haul stone and prepare plaster, donating thousands of hours. About a year after the dedication, Sagwitch and four others spent four days in the finished temple performing ordinances for family members killed at Bear River.

Symbolism & Design
  • The castellated form, with battlements, squared towers, and a fortress silhouette, is the visual signature Logan shares with Manti and with almost nothing else in the temple system.
  • The exterior was originally painted a pinkish off-white to conceal the dark, rough-hewn limestone underneath. The paint was allowed to weather away in the early 1900s, and the exposed stone became the building's defining feature.
  • Rows of arched windows in white frames run the length of both long elevations.

Changes Over Time
  • December 4, 1917: fire broke out on the temple's east side, traced to faulty wiring in a switchboard inside a closet beneath the main stairway. It damaged walls, carpet, furniture, windows, and paintings. Members repaired it in about three months.
  • 1976: closed for a complete interior reconstruction. The interior was gutted and the roof removed, leaving only the exterior walls and interior floors. The hand-painted murals and pioneer craftsmanship were lost, and the progressive muraled rooms were replaced with stationary rooms equipped for film. President Kimball, who rededicated the building, regretted the loss.
  • 1979: reopened after a public open house that drew 213,184 guests against an expected 90,000. There were 19,205 on the busiest day, with the line stretching seven blocks.
  • 2009: grounds renovated. A 1970s water feature gave way to an oval reflecting pool, and heated sidewalks were added for Cache Valley snow.
  • April 2019: President Nelson announced that Logan, among other pioneer-era temples, would be renovated. Plans have not been released.

Trivia
  • Between the 1884 dedication and the 1976 closure, 26,258,390 ordinances were performed here, more than 18 percent of all temple work in the Church at that time.
  • The first temple built with progressive muraled ordinance rooms for a live-acted endowment presentation.
  • One sitting and four future Presidents of the Church spoke at the 1979 rededication: Spencer W. Kimball, Ezra Taft Benson, Howard W. Hunter, Gordon B. Hinckley, and Thomas S. Monson.
  • In 1897 a two-story stone barn was built a block east to stable the animals of traveling patrons. Automobiles made it obsolete by the 1910s. It was placed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1985 and still stands at 368 East 200 North.

Manhattan New York Temple

Status
Closed since March 2, 2024, for a renovation the First Presidency projected would take about three years. Dates for the public open house and rededication have not been announced. Patrons have been directed to the Philadelphia Pennsylvania and Hartford Connecticut temples in the meantime.

Location
New York, New York. The temple occupies part of a Church-owned building at 125 Columbus Avenue on the Upper West Side, across the street from Lincoln Center and the Juilliard School, on a site of roughly a third of an acre. It takes its name from the borough of Manhattan; the postal city is New York, which is why the caption reads NEW YORK, NEW YORK.

Temple Number
The 119th dedicated temple.

Announced
August 7, 2002. The plan was to convert floors of an existing Church-owned building rather than to build new, following the approach used in Hong Kong.

Groundbreaking
September 23, 2002. Elder Spencer J. Condie of the Seventy presided.

Dedicated
June 13, 2004, by President Gordon B. Hinckley in four sessions, with Elder Robert D. Hales assisting.

Architecture
Built inside the shell of the six-story New York New York Stake Center, originally dedicated in the mid 1970s. About 20,630 square feet across the first, second, fifth, and sixth floors, with the chapel, classrooms, and offices remaining on the third and fourth. Roughly 80 feet tall, with a single attached corner spire carrying an angel Moroni statue. The original exterior was lightly variegated gray granite; the current renovation reclads the building in travertine.

Ordinance Rooms
Two instruction rooms, two sealing rooms, and one baptistry.

Construction Story
  • President Gordon B. Hinckley walked the property on March 23, 2002, and wrote in his journal that day that he felt enthusiastic about converting the upper portion of the building into a temple. He read the entry back to members at a fireside two years later.
  • He promised members that "within two years we will have a temple here for dedication." The dedication came in June 2004, which he acknowledged was roughly two years later.
  • The conversion had to fit a working stake center around a temple in the same building, leaving the chapel, classrooms, and administrative offices in place on two middle floors.
  • The public open house ran May 8 through June 5, 2004, drawing more than 53,000 visitors and coverage from national and international news outlets.

Symbolism & Design
  • The gray granite facade was chosen to sit comfortably beside Lincoln Center for the Arts and Juilliard directly across the street, rather than to stand apart from them.
  • The temple interior is soundproofed against the noise of the street outside, a design requirement that a freestanding temple on open ground would never have faced.
  • No angel Moroni stood on the building at dedication. The statue was attached on October 9, 2004, nearly four months later.

Changes Over Time
  • The First Presidency announced the current renovation in August 2023, and the temple closed the following March.
  • Released renderings show a substantially different exterior: building-height art glass, a golden spire, and a visitors' center with a statue of Jesus Christ. The meetinghouse on the third floor is being upgraded as part of the same work.

Trivia
  • Local members call it the "Miracle in Manhattan."
  • When the open house and dedication were announced in March 2004, the Church operated 117 temples worldwide and counted more than 62,000 members in the New York area.
  • The temple sits on a site of about a third of an acre, a fraction of the ground a freestanding temple occupies, and reaches its square footage by stacking rather than spreading.

Temple facts verified as of August 19, 2026.

Manti Utah Temple

Location
Manti, Utah. The temple stands at 200 East 510 North on a 27-acre site atop the oolite hill it was quarried from, visible for miles across the Sanpete Valley at an elevation of 5,657 feet.

Temple Number
Third among the Church's operating temples, after St. George and Logan.

Announced
June 25, 1875, by Brigham Young, who selected the hill north of town as the site.

Groundbreaking
April 25, 1877. Brigham Young presided at the site dedication, one of his last public acts before his death that August. Excavation crews began work that October.

Dedicated
May 17, 1888, in a private service where President Wilford Woodruff offered the dedicatory prayer, followed by public sessions May 21 to 23, 1888, at which Lorenzo Snow read the prayer to roughly 5,400 people.

Rededicated
June 14 to 16, 1985, by President Gordon B. Hinckley in nine sessions attended by 19,786, and again on April 21, 2024, by President Russell M. Nelson in a single evening session.

Architecture
William H. Folsom, architect, who also designed the Salt Lake Tabernacle. Castellated design in cream-colored oolite limestone quarried from the hill on which the temple stands, with two octagonal end towers, the taller rising 179 feet, and 74,792 square feet of floor area.

Ordinance Rooms
Four instruction rooms arranged for the progressive presentation, eight sealing rooms, and one baptistry.

First Temple President
Daniel H. Wells, who served from 1888 to 1891.

Construction Story
  • The stone came from the building's own foundation. Settlers had carved shelters for their first winter out of the creamy oolite of the hill, and the temple was later cut from the same rock.
  • Eleven years passed between the site dedication in 1877 and the dedication in 1888.
  • The temple cost $991,991.81. The Sanpete Stake raised $274,815.05 of that total from a farming community of modest means.
  • Some of the workmen walked or drove the seven miles from Ephraim, arriving Monday morning and going home Saturday evening, week after week, for years.

Symbolism & Design
  • Twin octagonal towers anchor the east and west ends, each enclosing a self-supporting spiral staircase that climbs without a central column.
  • The instruction rooms carry hand-painted murals rather than film backdrops. C.C.A. Christensen painted the creation room in the nineteenth century, with erupting volcanoes and dinosaurs among the scenes.
  • Minerva Teichert painted the world room, opening at the Tower of Babel and moving through history toward a Zion community, with indigenous figures on the west wall.
  • Danquart Weggeland painted the original garden room. After plaster damage in 1944 the room was repainted by Joseph Everett and finished by Robert L. Shepherd, who also painted the baptistry murals in 1946.

Changes Over Time
  • Lightning struck the temple in 1928.
  • A renovation completed in 1985 ran four years, and President Gordon B. Hinckley rededicated the building that June.
  • The temple closed October 2, 2021, for a renovation that strengthened the foundation, replaced mechanical, electrical and plumbing systems, added waterproofing, and built a new entrance and gathering space.
  • The First Presidency's March 2021 announcement had planned to remove the murals and move instruction to a single room. That decision was publicly reversed on May 1, 2021, when President Nelson said the pioneer craftsmanship, artwork and character would be preserved, murals included. Art conservators then cleaned and repaired them in place.
  • Video projectors were installed in the instruction rooms during the same renovation, ending the live narration the temple had used since 1888 and making the presentation available in more than 80 languages.

Trivia
  • Manti presented the endowment live for 133 years, longer than any other temple.
  • Its murals are the only ones in a temple that date from the pioneer period.
  • President Nelson's appearance at the 2024 rededication was a surprise. Elder Ronald A. Rasband had been announced to preside, and Nelson's own pioneer ancestors helped settle the Sanpete Valley.

Mexico City Mexico Temple

Location
Mexico City, Mexico. The temple stands in the Colonia San Juan de Aragón district of northeastern Mexico City, near the Bosque de Aragón, at an elevation of about 7,305 feet.

Temple Number
The 26th dedicated temple, and the first built in Mexico.

Announced
April 3, 1976, following President Spencer W. Kimball's meeting with Mexican Church leaders the month before.

Groundbreaking
November 25, 1979. Elder Boyd K. Packer of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles presided.

Dedicated
December 2 to 4, 1983, by President Gordon B. Hinckley in nine sessions. It was his second temple dedication in North America.

Rededicated
November 16, 2008, by President Thomas S. Monson in two sessions, after a renovation of about 19 months. Rededicated again September 13, 2015, by President Henry B. Eyring in three sessions, following an interior remodel and exterior cleaning.

Architecture
Originally designed by Church architect Emil B. Fetzer; the 2007 to 2008 renovation was handled by Valentiner Crane Brunjes Onyon of Salt Lake City. The exterior is white cast stone worked into adaptations of ancient Mesoamerican forms: a rectangular base, a basket weave band, and stepped levels that diminish as they rise. About 35,551 square feet, standing 151 feet to the top of the building, with a 15.5 foot angel Moroni statue above that.

Ordinance Rooms
Four instruction rooms, eleven sealing rooms, and one baptistry.

Construction Story
  • Before the temple opened, members in Mexico traveled roughly 1,500 miles to the Mesa Arizona Temple.
  • The public open house ran November 9 through November 19, 1983, and drew more than 120,000 visitors, with as many as 20,000 coming on a single day.
  • One visitor returned with 29 friends and asked permission to bring a hundred more.
  • Marble used in the building was quarried in Spain and fabricated in China.

Symbolism & Design
  • A basket weave pattern encircles the exterior, one of several motifs drawn from ancient Mesoamerican building traditions rather than from the Church's standard temple vocabulary.
  • The Mesoamerican reference carries inside as well, in carved carpet in the celestial room and in the art glass.
  • Millwork in the building includes carved columns worked with a waterfall design. The oak and cast bronze doors were installed in 2015.

Changes Over Time
  • Mexico City's ground is subsiding, and the temple has gone down with it. By the temple's 25th anniversary the building had dropped at least eight feet in elevation.
  • The temple closed in March 2007 for about 19 months. The work included seismic strengthening, foundation work to fortify the structure, replacement of the precast concrete exterior panels with panels matching the original, refurbishment of the angel Moroni statue, new landscaping, and remodeling of the baptistry, lobby, corridors, sealing rooms, and ordinance rooms.
  • A further interior remodel and exterior cleaning preceded the 2015 rededication.

Trivia
  • Five and a half years after the dedication, on July 25, 1989, Mexico became the first country outside the United States with 100 stakes.
  • The temple district serves more than 384,000 members across Mexico City and eleven surrounding states.
  • It was the first of what has grown to more than two dozen temples in Mexico.

Monticello Utah Temple

Location
Monticello, Utah, in San Juan County in the southeast corner of the state.

Temple Number
The 53rd dedicated temple, and the eleventh built in Utah.

Announced
October 4, 1997, as the first of the smaller temples President Gordon B. Hinckley had introduced earlier that year.

Groundbreaking
November 17, 1997. Elder Ben B. Banks presided.

Dedicated
July 26 to 27, 1998, by President Gordon B. Hinckley.

Rededicated
November 17, 2002, by President Gordon B. Hinckley, after the building was enlarged.

Architecture
Turkish off white marble. 11,225 square feet following the 2002 expansion, up from 7,000 as originally built, rising 66 feet to a single attached spire with an angel Moroni statue.

Ordinance Rooms
Two instruction rooms, two sealing rooms, one baptistry.

Construction Story
  • This was the first of the small temples, a design President Gordon B. Hinckley announced in 1997 to put temples within reach of members far from the existing ones.
  • The plan left out the laundry, the cafeteria and other space not needed for ordinances. That made the building far smaller and much faster to put up.
  • It went from groundbreaking to dedication in just over eight months, faster than any temple built before it.
  • As first completed, at 7,000 square feet, it had less than half the floor space of an ordinary meetinghouse.

Symbolism & Design
  • The exterior is clad in Turkish off white marble.
  • The first angel Moroni statue placed here was white fiberglass and stood six feet tall, against the twelve foot gold leafed figures used on earlier temples.

Changes Over Time
  • The temple was enlarged and remodeled in 2002, growing from 7,000 to 11,225 square feet, with a second instruction room and a second sealing room added. Temple president Lisle G. Adams explained the reason plainly: "The facilities we had were just not adequate to take care of the work that was being done."
  • President Hinckley rededicated the enlarged building on November 17, 2002, having dedicated the original four years earlier.
  • The white statue was later replaced with a gold leafed one.

Trivia
  • It was the first of the small temples, a design the Church has used many times since.
  • The temple was dedicated less than ten months after it was announced.

Nauvoo Illinois Temple

Location
Nauvoo, Illinois. The temple stands at 50 North Wells Street on a high bluff overlooking a bend in the Mississippi River, rebuilt on the same footprint as the original 1846 temple.

Temple Number
The Church's 113th operating temple at its dedication.

Announced
April 4, 1999, by President Gordon B. Hinckley.

Groundbreaking
October 24, 1999. President Gordon B. Hinckley presided. The cornerstone was laid November 5, 2000.

Dedicated
June 27 to June 30, 2002, by President Gordon B. Hinckley, in 13 sessions attended by 19,958 members in Nauvoo and carried by satellite to about 2,300 locations in 72 countries, in 38 languages.

Architecture
FFKR Architecture of Salt Lake City, Roger P. Jackson, principal architect; Legacy Constructors, contractor. The exterior recreates William Weeks's design for the original temple, developed in collaboration with Joseph Smith: limestone quarried in Russellville, Alabama, laid over a reinforced concrete structure, rising 162 feet 5 inches, with approximately 54,000 square feet of floor area.

Ordinance Rooms
Five instruction rooms in a progressive design, a celestial room, six sealing rooms, an assembly room, and a baptistry with the font resting on twelve oxen, duplicating the font of the original temple.

First Temple President
Richard W. Winder, called as the temple's first president for its 2002 opening, with Barbara W. Winder as matron.

Construction Story
  • The original temple rose over five hard years: cornerstones laid April 6, 1841, first endowments administered December 10, 1845, and more than 6,000 Latter-day Saints endowed by early February 1846, even as the first wagons rolled west out of the city.
  • The Saints dedicated the original as they were leaving it: privately by Joseph Young on April 30, 1846, and publicly the next day, with Orson Hyde offering the first public dedicatory prayer. An arsonist's fire gutted the building on October 9, 1848; the Icarians, a communal group newly arrived in Nauvoo, purchased the temple block in April 1849; a tornado toppled much of the remaining stonework on May 27, 1850.
  • President Gordon B. Hinckley announced the rebuild on April 4, 1999, and the new temple was raised on the same footprint as the original building.
  • A historical research team of about ten people, chaired by historian Glen M. Leonard, worked from historical drawings and journals; more than 14,000 exterior stones were individually designed, and an average sunstone took 300 hours to carve.
  • F. Keith Stepan, managing director of the Church's Temple Construction Department, reported a construction quality evaluation of 99, the highest his department had ever received, and called it the most well-built temple he had worked on.

Symbolism & Design
  • Thirty sunstones, carved replicas of the originals, crown the exterior pilasters; each pilaster also carries a moonstone at its base and a starstone above the sunstone.
  • Both the temple and its angel Moroni statue face west.
  • Stepan estimated the finished reconstruction to be about 95 percent correct to the 1846 original.

Trivia
  • The first dedicatory session began at 6 p.m. on June 27, 2002; President Hinckley noted that the hour corresponded to 5 p.m. in Joseph Smith's era, 158 years, almost to the hour, after the martyrdom of Joseph and Hyrum Smith at Carthage Jail.
  • The coverstone bears the inscription "Originally built 1846. Rebuilt 2002."
  • The public open house ran May 6 to June 22, 2002, except Sundays, and drew 331,849 visitors.
  • Lightning struck the angel Moroni statue on June 28, 2019; a newly gilded replacement statue was set atop the tower on November 12, 2019.

Oakland California Temple

Location
Oakland, California. The temple stands on an 18.1 acre hillside site at 4770 Lincoln Avenue in the Oakland hills, with commanding views west across San Francisco Bay.

Temple Number
The 13th dedicated temple, and the second built in California.

Announced
January 23, 1961, by President David O. McKay.

Groundbreaking
May 26, 1962. President David O. McKay presided, joined by his counselors in the First Presidency.

Dedicated
November 17 to 19, 1964, by President David O. McKay in six sessions. More than 120 general authorities and their spouses attended.

Rededicated
June 16, 2019, by President Dallin H. Oaks in three sessions, accompanied by Elder David A. Bednar.

Architecture
Designed by Harold W. Burton, who spent a career designing buildings for the Church and worked the idiom of the early 1960s into this one. Reinforced concrete faced with Sierra white granite quarried at Raymond, California. About 95,000 square feet, with five spires: a central tower reaching 170 feet surrounded by four smaller ones.

Ordinance Rooms
Four instruction rooms, seven sealing rooms, and one baptistry.

Construction Story
  • The building was completed on September 27, 1964, a little over two years after ground was broken.
  • The public open house ran October 5 through October 31, 1964, and was extended an additional week. About 347,000 people toured the temple.
  • Its dedication made California the second state in the country with more than one temple.
  • The 2018 renovation drew materials from across the world: flooring stone from Greece, China, and Georgia, primavera wood from South America for the celestial room doors, ribbon striped mahogany from Africa in some sealing rooms, and custom bronze hardware made from Indian brass.

Symbolism & Design
  • The five spire arrangement is the building's signature, and it is a deliberate borrowing. Burton's design points toward sacred architecture of the Far East, the Taj Mahal and Angkor Wat among them, chosen to reflect the range of people living in Northern California.
  • Two granite relief panels, each about 35 feet by 13 feet, carry the building's narrative. The north panel depicts Christ teaching, drawn from Matthew 5 and 6. The south panel depicts the resurrected Savior appearing to the Nephites, from 3 Nephi 11.
  • A cascading waterfall and creek style water feature runs through the gardens at the front of the temple.

Changes Over Time
  • The original waterfall was removed in 1969 because the leaks could not be repaired. Modern materials made it possible to restore it during the renovation fifty years later.
  • The temple closed in February 2018 for a renovation of about 16 months, followed by a public open house May 11 through June 1, 2019.

Trivia
  • It was the first temple in the United States designed for a film presentation of the endowment, and the first with multiple instruction rooms feeding into a central celestial room. Nearly every temple built since has followed that plan.
  • The front doors malfunctioned shortly after the 1964 dedication, and patrons used a side entrance for years afterward.
  • The interstake center on the grounds, built in 1959, once served as the practice facility for the Golden State Warriors.

Status
This drawing shows the temple as it stood from its 1972 dedication until it closed for renovation on April 2, 2011. Ogden, Utah, on 9.96 acres occupying a full downtown block along Washington Boulevard.

Temple Number

Announced
August 24, 1967, alongside a companion temple for Provo.

Groundbreaking

Ordinance Rooms

Provo Utah Temple (1972–2024)

Status
This building no longer stands. It closed on February 24, 2024, and was taken down rather than renovated. A replacement, the Provo Utah Rock Canyon Temple, is under construction on the same hill, set west of the original foundation where the slope is flatter. Everything below describes the 1972 building.

Location
Provo, Utah. A 17-acre site on the east bench at the mouth of Rock Canyon, overlooking the city, Utah Lake, and the length of Utah Valley. Brigham Young University bordered the grounds to the southwest, and the Provo Missionary Training Center stood across the street.

Temple Number
The 15th dedicated temple in operation. It was the sixth temple built in Utah and the first in Utah County.

Announced
August 14, 1967, by Hugh B. Brown and N. Eldon Tanner of the First Presidency, in a meeting with 28 local stake presidencies. It was the first Utah temple announced after the Salt Lake Temple was dedicated in 1893, a gap of nearly 75 years.

Groundbreaking
September 15, 1969. Hugh B. Brown broke ground and Joseph Fielding Smith dedicated the site the same day. The cornerstone was set on May 21, 1971, while the building was still going up.

Dedicated
February 9, 1972, by Joseph Fielding Smith, in two sessions. President Smith presided but asked Harold B. Lee to read the prayer he had written. More than 70,000 people attended, because the sessions were carried by closed-circuit television to the Marriott Center and four other venues on the BYU campus.

Architecture
Emil B. Fetzer, Church architect. Modern and functional. White cast stone with gold anodized aluminum grilles and bronze glass panels, set as a flat round base with a single spire rising from the center. 130,825 square feet across four floors, standing 175 feet high, of which the spire accounted for 118 feet.

Ordinance Rooms
Six ordinance rooms, arranged so a new session could begin every 20 minutes, along with a celestial room, twelve sealing rooms, and a baptistry on the below-ground floor.

First Temple President
Harold Glen Clark, 1972 to 1976, with Mary Deane Peterson Gilbert Clark as matron.

Construction Story
  • The decision came out of arithmetic. By the mid-1960s roughly 52 percent of all ordinance work in the Church was being performed in three buildings: Logan, Manti, and Salt Lake. Temples for Provo and Ogden were announced in 1967 to take the load off them.
  • Fetzer designed both under a single basic plan, with efficiency, convenience, and economical construction as the stated priorities. The two buildings went up at the same time and were nearly identical until Ogden was given a new exterior in the early 2010s.
  • Provo's groundbreaking came one week after Ogden's, the first time two temple groundbreakings were held in the same month.
  • Several thousand people turned out on May 21, 1971, for the cornerstone ceremony, with the walls and spire already standing.

Symbolism & Design
  • Circulation drove the plan. Six ordinance rooms ringed a celestial room at the center of the top floor, and a corridor ran the full circle of the top two levels. Fetzer took the loop from a park in Copenhagen encircled by an elliptical roadway. Patrons moved through without crossing paths, and Church News noted it was almost impossible to get lost inside.
  • The original design called for a gold-leafed angel Moroni on the gold spire. The statue was dropped before the building was finished.
  • Many members read the white base as the pillar of cloud and the gold spire as the pillar of fire from Exodus. That reading did not come from the design team. Fred Baker, who worked closely with Fetzer, said flatly that "we didn't have any symbolism in mind" and that the work was focused on what happened inside the building. Church News published a correction to that effect in 2024, citing Richard Cowan.

Changes Over Time
  • The building opened as simply the Provo Temple. It became the Provo Utah Temple in 1999, when the Church revised its temple naming convention.
  • In May 2003, 31 years after dedication, an angel Moroni statue was placed on the spire and the spire was repainted from gold to white. That is the version most people photographed.
  • In the October 2021 general conference, Russell M. Nelson announced the reconstruction of the temple following the dedication of the Orem Utah Temple. An exterior rendering of the redesign was released in November 2021, and the closure date was announced in June 2023.
  • On February 20, 2024, the First Presidency announced that the rebuilt temple would carry a new name, the Provo Utah Rock Canyon Temple. The original closed four days later and demolition followed.

Trivia
  • For decades this was the busiest temple in the Church. In 1973, its first full year of operation, 17.7 percent of all ordinances performed worldwide were performed here.
  • Richard Cowan and Justin Bray called it the "working temple." It ran as many as 50 endowment sessions a day, the first starting at 5:30 a.m. and the last ending near 11:00 p.m. In 1976 it set a record with 76,000 endowments completed in a single month.
  • The public open house ran January 8 to 29, 1972, and drew 246,201 visitors. Special tours were arranged for groups with particular needs, including one for visually impaired guests, whom the temple president led through while describing the building aloud.
  • Sessions in Spanish and sessions for patrons who were hearing impaired both began in 1974. Portuguese, German, Japanese, Mandarin, and others followed, and by 2022 ordinances could be received here in 82 languages.

Provo City Center Temple

Location
Provo, Utah. The temple stands at 50 South University Avenue in downtown Provo, on the 5.6-acre city block where the Provo Tabernacle stood for more than a century.

Temple Number
The Church's 150th operating temple at its dedication, the 16th in Utah, and the second in Provo.

Announced
October 1, 2011, by President Thomas S. Monson in general conference, less than a year after fire destroyed the tabernacle's interior.

Groundbreaking
May 12, 2012. Elder Jeffrey R. Holland of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles presided.

Dedicated
March 20, 2016, by Elder Dallin H. Oaks of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles, in three sessions; President Russell M. Nelson presided at the third session.

Architecture
FFKR Architects, architect; Jacobsen Construction Company, contractor. The restored brick shell of the 1898 Provo Tabernacle forms the exterior, with arched art-glass windows, corner towers, and blue conical roofs, enclosing 85,084 square feet of floor area and rising 150 feet.

Ordinance Rooms
Three instruction rooms in a two-stage progressive presentation, five sealing rooms, and a baptistry with an oval font of rose gold granite.

First Temple President
Allen C. Ostergar Jr., called as the temple's first president for its 2016 opening.

Construction Story
  • In the early morning of December 17, 2010, a four-alarm fire gutted the Provo Tabernacle, the pioneer-era landmark begun in 1882 and dedicated in 1898. Investigators concluded the blaze was accidental, traced to a 300-watt light fixture left resting on a wooden speaker enclosure in the attic. The brick walls survived; nearly everything inside did not.
  • On October 1, 2011, President Thomas S. Monson announced in general conference: "After careful study, we have decided to rebuild it, with full preservation and restoration of the exterior, to become the second temple of the Church in the city of Provo."
  • To build new levels beneath the historic shell, crews reinforced the fire-scarred walls with concrete and carried them on more than 300 metal stilts while excavating 40 feet below.
  • Thousands gathered on March 31, 2014, to watch a 13-foot angel Moroni statue set on the center tower. No formal ceremony was planned; the crowd came anyway.
  • Construction finished on December 17, 2015, five years to the day after the fire.

Symbolism & Design
  • Wood moldings, newel posts, art glass, finials, and hardware salvaged from the tabernacle were worked back into the temple, and the tabernacle's original pulpit now stands in the temple's chapel.
  • The Victorian-style interior carries floral motifs in African mahogany and walnut, and stenciling patterns documented on the tabernacle's charred walls informed the design of the bride's dressing room.
  • An early-1900s stained-glass depiction of Christ, reclaimed from a demolished Presbyterian church in New York, was installed in the temple.

Trivia
  • Church News reported that a replica painting depicting the Second Coming was recovered from the fire, burned through except for the image of Christ near its center; the charred canvas passed into the Church's keeping.
  • The tabernacle hosted sessions of general conference in 1886 and 1887, and U.S. President William Howard Taft spoke there on September 24, 1909.
  • More than 800,000 visitors toured the temple during its seven-week open house, and on the eve of dedication 4,500 youth performed a cultural celebration titled "Beauty from Ashes."
  • At the cornerstone ceremony, 12-year-old Dylan Edwards and his 7-year-old sister Malaia were invited to finish applying the mortar.

Dedicated
March 24, 2024, by President Henry B. Eyring of the First Presidency, in two sessions.

Architecture

Ordinance Rooms

J. Kevin Ence, with matron Debbie Ence.

Construction Story
  • Five and a half years passed between the announcement and the dedication.
  • The public open house ran February 1 through March 2, 2024, excluding Sundays.

Symbolism & Design
  • The exterior takes its motifs from the cottonwood trees, mountains and canyons of southern Utah, with stylized cottonwood leaves worked into the precast panels.

  • Interior stonework is laid in horizontal bands that echo the strata in the cliffs and canyons nearby.
  • Palm trees line the entrance walk.

Rome Italy Temple

Location
Rome, Italy. The temple stands on an elevated 15 acre site on Via di Settebagni in northeast Rome, beside the Grande Raccordo Anulare that rings the city. The grounds also hold a visitors' center, a meetinghouse, a family history center, and patron housing.

Temple Number
The 162nd dedicated temple, the first in Italy, and the thirteenth in Europe.

Announced
October 4, 2008, by President Thomas S. Monson during general conference.

Groundbreaking
October 23, 2010. President Thomas S. Monson presided.

Dedicated
March 10 to 12, 2019, by President Russell M. Nelson in seven sessions. President Nelson conducted the cornerstone ceremony on the first day.

Architecture
Designed by Niels Valentiner. A Bianco Sardo granite facade over cast in place concrete, three stories and about 40,000 square feet, standing 156 feet 3 inches with two attached end spires and an angel Moroni statue. Interiors are finished in Perlato Svevo and Cenia marble, sapele, burl and cherry wood, with light fixtures of Murano glass from Venice.

Ordinance Rooms
Two instruction rooms, three sealing rooms, and one baptistry.

Construction Story
  • Eight and a half years passed between the groundbreaking in 2010 and the dedication in 2019, one of the longer builds of the modern era.
  • The temple was built on a former farm, and olive trees between 400 and 500 years old already stood on the ground when the site was chosen.
  • The public open house ran January 14 through February 16, 2019. About 52,000 people toured the temple. Elder David A. Bednar and Elder Ronald A. Rasband led the first tours for journalists.
  • The angel Moroni statue was installed on March 25, 2017, two years before the dedication.

Symbolism & Design
  • The oval piazza and the curves of the building take their cue from Roman architecture, and specifically from Borromini's church of San Carlo alle Quattro Fontane, known in the city as San Carlino.
  • Floor patterns inside the temple are drawn from Michelangelo's paving at the Piazza del Campidoglio.
  • A floor to ceiling art glass wall at the entrance depicts a scene from the life of Christ. Other windows take their forms from the olive trees on the site, which carry their own association with the Resurrection.

Trivia
  • On March 11, 2019, the entire First Presidency and Quorum of the Twelve Apostles gathered in the temple's visitors' center. It was the first time the two bodies had assembled together anywhere outside the United States.
  • The visitors' center holds digitally replicated statues of Jesus Christ and the Twelve Apostles, based on the originals Bertel Thorvaldsen carved in the 1800s, along with a fountain representing living water.
  • The dedication came nearly 170 years after Lorenzo Snow began missionary work in Italy in 1850. Writing of that beginning, Snow said he had "opened a door which no man can shut." He also recorded, in an account published in 1851, that "the work here is slow and tedious. Nevertheless, the Church has been established. The tree has been planted and is spreading its roots."
  • The day before the dedication began, on March 9, 2019, President Nelson met with Pope Francis at the Vatican, the first formal audience between a president of the Church and a pope.

That's why I started this company. It doesn't take much for someone who has been prepared to tap you on the shoulder and ask a question that changes the direction of their life. No argument, no pitch, no lesson plan. Just an opening.

- Evan

Salt Lake Temple

Location
Salt Lake City, Utah. The temple stands on the 10-acre Temple Square in downtown Salt Lake City, at 50 West North Temple Street, at an elevation of 4,335 feet. Status: closed for renovation since December 29, 2019; a public open house is scheduled for April 5 to October 1, 2027, and no rededication date had been announced as of August 17, 2026.

Temple Number
The Church's fourth dedicated temple in operation.

Announced
July 28, 1847, when Brigham Young designated the site four days after the pioneer company entered the Salt Lake Valley.

Groundbreaking
February 14, 1853. Brigham Young presided and broke ground, and Heber C. Kimball dedicated the site. Cornerstones were laid April 6, 1853.

Dedicated
April 6, 1893, by President Wilford Woodruff, in the first of 31 dedicatory sessions held through April 24. Sessions ran twice daily, with special sessions for children.

Architecture
Truman O. Angell, Church architect, designed the temple in collaboration with Brigham Young; after Angell's death in 1887, Joseph Don Carlos Young completed the spires and interior, incorporating a steel frame, electric lighting, steam heating, and elevators. Six-spire design faced in quartz monzonite from Little Cottonwood Canyon, 20 miles southeast of the site. The footprint measures about 119 by 181 feet, with walls nine feet thick at the base tapering to six feet at the top. The east center spire rises 210 feet, and 222.5 feet to the top of the 12.5-foot angel Moroni statue. With more than 253,000 square feet of floor area, it is the Church's largest temple.

Ordinance Rooms
As reconfigured in the current renovation: five instruction rooms seating 150 each, where the endowment is presented by film in a single room rather than the live, room-to-room presentation used before the closure; a separate veil room; ten added sealing rooms, for an announced total of 23; and two baptistries, the second added during the renovation.

First Temple President
Lorenzo Snow, called as the temple's first president for its 1893 opening. He served until becoming President of the Church in September 1898.

Construction Story
  • Defects discovered in the original foundation forced workers to remove and replace portions of the basement walls, delaying construction by about five years. Brigham Young set the standard in 1863: "I want to see the temple built in a manner that it will endure through the Millennium."
  • For the first two decades, stone was hauled 20 miles from Little Cottonwood Canyon by wagon team; the railroad's arrival in the 1870s finally gave builders a faster and more reliable way to move it.
  • The capstone was laid April 6, 1892, before an estimated 40,000 people, with Lorenzo Snow leading the Hosanna Shout with waving white handkerchiefs in the form still used at temple dedications. The angel Moroni statue was placed on the east center spire at the same ceremony.
  • The dedication followed exactly one year after the capstone, with the temple's ornate interior finished in that single intervening year.

Symbolism & Design
  • Carved stones ascend the buttresses in sequence: earthstones at the base, each weighing about 3.5 tons; moonstones depicting the moon in its phases, which Orson Pratt sketched from his observatory on the temple block; and sunstones cut with 52 points, one for each week of the year.
  • The west center tower carries a carving of the Big Dipper, its pointer stars indicating the position of the North Star.
  • The center towers bear carvings of clasped hands and the all-seeing eye, and two cloudstones on the east center tower show rays of light breaking through dark clouds.
  • Cyrus Dallin's 12.5-foot angel Moroni, hammered from copper and overlaid with 22-karat gold leaf, crowns the east center spire; a heavy counterweight suspended inside the spire allows the statue to sway slightly in the wind.

Changes Over Time
  • The temple closed from July 29, 1962, to May 21, 1963, for extensive updating, and an annex opened in 1966.
  • On April 19, 2019, President Russell M. Nelson announced the current renovation; the temple closed December 29, 2019, for structural and seismic work centered on a base isolation system, with new north entry pavilions and a skylit grand hall through which patrons will enter.
  • A magnitude 5.7 earthquake on March 18, 2020, shook the trumpet from the angel Moroni statue's hand and displaced some smaller spire stones. The statue and capstone, about 5,000 pounds together, were removed by crane on May 18, 2020, and the refurbished statue returned to the spire on April 2, 2024.
  • In March 2021, the First Presidency announced the move from live endowment sessions to single-room film presentations, along with the added instruction rooms, sealing rooms, and second baptistry.
  • Renovation completion is projected for the end of 2026. President Nelson announced the public open house on February 14, 2025; it runs April 5 to October 1, 2027, with free tickets available on TempleSquare.org beginning September 1, 2026. No rededication date had been announced as of August 17, 2026.

Trivia
  • After 40 years of construction, the masonry was so precise that the south wall differed in height from the north wall by one-eighth of an inch across the temple's 181-foot length.
  • On April 5, 1893, the evening before the dedication began, about 5,000 invited guests, most of them not Church members, toured the finished temple.
  • The 1892 capstone held a time capsule that was opened in 2020, 128 years after its placement, following the statue's removal.

Temple facts verified as of August 17, 2026.

San Antonio, Texas. The temple sits on about 5.5 acres atop a prominent hill in the Stone Oak area of north San Antonio, at an elevation of 1,225 feet.

Temple Number
The Church's 120th operating temple at its dedication.

Announced
June 24, 2001. The site was announced August 19, 2002.

Groundbreaking
March 29, 2003. Elder H. Bruce Stucki of the Seventy presided and dedicated the site.

Dedicated
May 22, 2005, by President Gordon B. Hinckley, in four sessions attended by 14,069 members.

Architecture
Rehler, Vaughn & Koone, architects; Jacobsen Construction, contractor. Traditional single-spire design with a granite exterior, 97 feet wide by 191 feet long, rising 115 feet to the top of the angel Moroni statue, with approximately 16,800 square feet of floor area.

Ordinance Rooms
Two instruction rooms in a two-stage progressive design, two sealing rooms, and a baptistry with the font resting on twelve oxen.

First Temple President
A. Ray Otte, called as the temple's first president for its 2005 opening.

  • Local members did not just watch the temple rise. Members of one Spanish-speaking branch came to the site and washed construction bricks, and members across the area hand-delivered 16-page open house brochures through their neighborhoods.
  • The 13-foot gold-leafed angel Moroni statue was placed atop the spire on September 21, 2004, eight months before the dedication.
  • The night before the dedication, local youth performed the Heart of Texas Youth Jubilee, a cultural celebration held at the Alamodome.

Symbolism & Design
  • The temple stands on one of the highest points in the area, and its lighted spire can be seen from roughly 30 miles away.
  • Every window carries art glass, and the grounds feature water features and landscaping chosen to reflect the rugged beauty of south Texas.
  • At the dedication, Elder Charles Didier called the hilltop setting deliberate, noting that temples built on elevated ground prompt elevated thoughts.

Trivia
  • It was the fourth temple built in Texas, following Dallas, Houston, and Lubbock.
  • The three-week open house drew 69,679 visitors between April 16 and May 7, 2005, with members organizing chartered buses from a local high school to handle the crowds.

- Evan

San Diego California Temple

Location
San Diego, California. The temple stands on a 7.2-acre site in northern San Diego near the La Jolla community, directly beside Interstate 5, at 7474 Charmant Drive. Its district serves about 50,000 members across San Diego County, southern Riverside County, and Yuma, Arizona.

Temple Number
The Church's 45th operating temple at its dedication.

Announced
April 7, 1984, by Gordon B. Hinckley, then a counselor in the First Presidency.

Groundbreaking
February 27, 1988. President Ezra Taft Benson presided and turned the first shovelful of sod; President Thomas S. Monson dedicated the site.

Dedicated
April 25 to 30, 1993, in 23 sessions by Presidents Gordon B. Hinckley and Thomas S. Monson, counselors in the First Presidency, attended by 49,273 people.

Renovated
Closed July 31, 2023, for an extensive renovation. A public open house ran June 18 to July 11, 2026, and the rededication is scheduled for August 23, 2026.

Architecture
William S. Lewis Jr., design architect; Dennis Hyndman, project architect; Shelly Hyndman, interior design architect. A four-story structure of structural steel and precast concrete finished in marblecrete plaster, rising 169 feet, with 58,005 square feet of floor area and ten spires: two central towers, each framed at its base by four smaller spires, with a gilded angel Moroni statue atop the eastern spire.

Ordinance Rooms
Four instruction rooms, six sealing rooms, and a baptistry.

First Temple President
Floyd L. Packard, called as the temple's first president for its 1993 opening, with Alice E. Packard as matron.

Construction Story
  • President Ezra Taft Benson presided at the 1988 groundbreaking and turned the first shovelful of sod himself, while his counselor Thomas S. Monson offered the site dedication.
  • The gilded angel Moroni statue was set atop the eastern spire on December 23, 1991, well over a year before the building opened.
  • The pre-dedication open house ran February 20 to April 3, 1993, and drew about 720,000 visitors, roughly 100,000 more than the 620,000 the Church had expected.

Symbolism & Design
  • Ten spires in all: two central towers, each ringed at its base by four smaller spires. When the renovated temple reopened in 2026, the Church described the ten-spire configuration as unlike any other of its temples in the world.
  • At the center of the building sits an atrium shaped as an eight-pointed star, formed by two overlapping squares offset 45 degrees and holding a garden, a rare feature among the Church's temples.
  • The white exterior glistens in direct sun because marble chips were blown into the wet plaster. Church historian Spencer McBride has compared the effect to the Church's first temple in Kirtland, Ohio, where early members mixed crushed china and glassware into the stucco for the same shimmer.
  • The celestial room rises through two levels and is lit by four chandeliers, with fixtures finished in satin gold and set with Asfour crystal; art glass throughout the building runs to gold and tan tones.

Changes Over Time
  • The 2023 to 2026 renovation replaced the aging art glass with insulated units, upgraded the heating and air conditioning systems, repaired the roof, added ADA-compliant bathrooms, and restored the marblecrete facade and landscaping.
  • The temple's cafeteria was removed, and the space became an 85-seat waiting room for guests attending weddings.
  • The 2026 open house was pitched to neighbors who had watched the building from the freeway for decades but never seen inside; the rededication that follows is scheduled for August 23, 2026.

Trivia
  • The third temple built in California, following Los Angeles (dedicated 1956) and Oakland (1964).
  • After the 1993 open house, the San Diego Press Club named the temple its 1993 Headliner of the Year, and the Church's open house effort earned a Silver Anvil Award from the Public Relations Society of America.
  • The building is a fixture of local curiosity coverage: The San Diego Union-Tribune counts it among the county's most recognizable landmarks, and a Fox 5 San Diego explainer answered viewers asking about "that castle-like building off the freeway."
  • At its dedication the temple district covered about 80,000 members in 21 stakes across four Southern California counties plus five stakes and a mission district in northern Mexico; today it serves about 50,000 members on the United States side of the border.

Saratoga Springs Utah Temple

Location
Saratoga Springs, Utah. The temple sits on a 22.71-acre site at 987 South Ensign Drive, on a bluff overlooking Utah Lake and the Wasatch Front in the city's Beacon Pointe area west of Redwood Road, at an elevation of 4,652 feet.

Temple Number
The Church's 179th dedicated temple. At its dedication it was the 18th temple in Utah and the fifth in Utah County.

Announced
April 2, 2017, by President Thomas S. Monson in his opening remarks at the Sunday morning session of the 187th Annual General Conference.

Groundbreaking
October 19, 2019. Elder Craig C. Christensen, General Authority Seventy and president of the Church's Utah Area, presided. Full construction began November 6, 2019.

Dedicated
August 13, 2023, by President Henry B. Eyring, Second Counselor in the First Presidency, in two sessions held at 10:00 a.m. and 1:30 p.m.

Architecture
Jacobsen Construction Company, architect and general contractor; Josh Stewart, Church architect; interior design by Naylor Wentworth Lund Architects. A three-story temple of 97,836 square feet rising 199 feet 9 inches to the top of the angel Moroni statue, with an exterior of eight-inch-thick beige precast concrete panels and a spire of glass fiber reinforced concrete.

Ordinance Rooms
Four instruction rooms, six sealing rooms, and a baptistry.

First Temple President
Lon W. Sorensen, with Marie Ellen Sorensen as matron. Their calls were announced in March 2022, ahead of the temple's 2023 opening.

Construction Story
  • The temple stands on ground the Lehi Utah Stake began working as a Church welfare dry farm in the 1950s. The land produced wheat, feed corn, and alfalfa hay for the Church's welfare efforts before it was selected for the temple.
  • The exterior concrete panels were cast in Salt Lake County by Forterra, and the spire was fabricated by Unlimited Design of Salt Lake City. The structure is steel with concrete shear walls and concrete floor slabs.
  • A 21,000-square-foot meetinghouse was built on the same site as the temple.
  • The public open house ran from April 15 to July 8, 2023, excluding Sundays, and drew 587,749 visitors.
  • Between the 2017 announcement and the 2023 dedication, the number of stakes in the Saratoga Springs, Eagle Mountain, and west Lehi area grew by 36 percent.

Symbolism & Design
  • A decorative band wrapping the exterior carries a mountain design, and metal panels depict Utah Lake wetlands and snowy egrets. The egret is a logo of Saratoga Springs City.
  • Holdman Studios of Lehi designed and manufactured the art glass, which references the Arts and Crafts movement and renders the colors and forms of Utah Lake and the Wasatch Mountains in purples, blues, greens, and golds.
  • The baptistry art glass depicts snowy egrets among wetland grasses, with wave patterns representing Utah Lake at the base of the panels, gold silhouettes of birds above the water, and stylized Wasatch peaks.
  • Stylized flowers in the decorative painting represent wildflowers found in the area, including the iris, daisy, and chrysanthemum, and painted lines of water and waves reference Utah Lake and the waters of the Wasatch Range.
  • Millwork and doors are Sapele African mahogany in an Art Deco style, and bronze door hardware made by Luna Bronze of Provo repeats the grass, wetland, and water motifs drawn from the art glass.

Trivia
  • It was one of five temples announced on April 2, 2017, alongside temples for Brasília Brazil, the greater Manila Philippines area, Nairobi Kenya, and Pocatello Idaho.
  • At its dedication, the Church noted it was the first of six temples scheduled for dedication within less than two months.
  • Saratoga Springs incorporated in December 1997 with 167 residents, and its first stake was created September 16, 2001. By the temple's completion, northwestern Utah County counted 20 stakes in Lehi, 9 in Saratoga Springs, and 9 in Eagle Mountain.
  • The temple's commissioned original artwork includes "Timpanogos from Across the Lake" by Bruce Brainard, "Evening Flight" by Adair Payne, and "Jordan River Sunrise" by Ken Stockton.

Under construction, with major construction complete and crews finishing the interior; furnishings began arriving in spring 2026. Dates for the public open house and dedication have not yet been announced. Michael L. Staheli and Linda A. Staheli of the Smithfield Utah North Stake were called in March 2026 as the temple's first president and matron.

Location
Smithfield, Utah. The temple stands on a 13.3-acre site at 800 West and 100 North in northern Cache Valley, at an elevation of 4,506 feet, roughly seven miles from the Logan Utah Temple.

Temple Number
The second temple in Cache County, following the Logan Utah Temple, dedicated in 1884. Its number among the Church's dedicated temples will be fixed at its dedication.

Announced
April 4, 2021, by President Russell M. Nelson during the 191st Annual General Conference, one of 20 temples announced that day.

Groundbreaking
June 18, 2022. Elder Quentin L. Cook of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles presided and dedicated the site, with Elder Gary E. Stevenson conducting. About 600 people attended in person, and the ceremony was broadcast to the 13 stakes of the temple district.

Architecture
A three-story temple of approximately 81,000 square feet. The exterior features columns of arched windows and arched entryways, with a tall domed cupola near the front of the building and a smaller dome at the opposite end.

Ordinance Rooms
Four instruction rooms, four sealing rooms, and two baptistries.

Construction Story
  • Ground was broken by two Apostles who grew up in Cache Valley. Elder Cook and Elder Stevenson are both Utah State University graduates, and Elder Cook told the gathering that the valley "always feels like home to me. It is among the most beautiful places on earth."
  • In the site dedicatory prayer, Elder Cook prayed that the temple would become "a beacon light for the communities it serves" and gave thanks "for those who have gone before us."
  • The temple rises on ground the LaMont Poulsen family farmed for more than 160 years before it became a temple site.
  • The main dome was set in June 2024 and the rear cupola that August; exterior stonework was substantially complete by the end of 2024.

Symbolism & Design

St. George Utah Temple

Location
St. George, Utah. The temple stands at 250 East 400 South on a 6.5-acre site near the city's historic district, a white landmark among the red sandstone buttes of southern Utah.

Temple Number
First among the Church's operating temples. It is the oldest operating temple of the Church and the first temple dedicated in Utah.

Announced
January 31, 1871, by Brigham Young in a meeting with the St. George Stake high council and other local leaders, the first temple proposed since the exodus from Nauvoo. Erastus Snow answered the news with a shout of "Glory, hallelujah!"

Groundbreaking
November 9, 1871. Brigham Young dedicated the site, and excavation began the same day.

Dedicated
April 6 to 8, 1877, with the dedicatory prayer offered by President Daniel H. Wells of the First Presidency in the opening session of general conference, held in the temple; Brigham Young presided and, despite failing health, offered brief remarks. Portions were dedicated January 1, 1877: the baptistry by Wilford Woodruff, an assembly room by Erastus Snow, and a sealing room by Brigham Young Jr. Baptisms for the dead began January 9 and endowments January 11, 1877.

Rededicated
November 11 to 12, 1975, by President Spencer W. Kimball following a major expansion, and again on December 10, 2023, by President Jeffrey R. Holland, Acting President of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles, in two sessions.

Architecture
Truman O. Angell, architect, appointed by Brigham Young. Native red sandstone quarried north of the city and plastered white, rising 175 feet, with 143,969 square feet of floor area following the 2019 to 2023 renovation.

Ordinance Rooms
Three instruction rooms with a separate veil room, seventeen sealing rooms, and a baptistry whose font bowl and oxen are the originals from 1877.

First Temple President
Wilford Woodruff, later President of the Church. Under Brigham Young's direction, he and others made the first written record of temple ordinances that had previously been passed on by word of mouth.

Construction Story
  • Early Saints packed the site with volcanic rock, using a cannon as a pile driver to compact the foundation.
  • The temple was built by local craftsmen from local materials. Stone and lime for plaster came from nearby quarries, timber came from Mount Trumbull, Arizona, which required building a new road, and window glass and metal for nails and the roof came from Salt Lake City.
  • Brigham Young personally paid for the baptismal font. Cast in six pieces at the Davis and Howe foundry in Salt Lake City, it traveled by rail to Nephi and then by ox team through the summer heat. A freighter recalled that Orson Hyde, seeing the font in place, "came out weeping with joy."
  • Members of the Paiute tribes, on whose historic homeland St. George sits, participated in the construction and in early ordinance work.
  • A few construction workers left signatures and time capsules in the walls; one contained original poetry they had written. St. George had roughly 1,100 residents when the work began.

Changes Over Time
  • The temple has been renovated more than 10 times since 1877.
  • Lightning damaged the original tower in August 1878. A taller replacement designed by architect William H. Folsom was completed in 1883, and in 1994 the wooden tower was replaced with one of fiberglass and metal.
  • A 1917 project enlarged the annex, and a 1938 remodel moved the endowment rooms from the basement to the main level, replacing a large assembly room with smaller mural rooms. Architects Don Carlos Young and Ramm Hansen designed both.
  • A 1975 renovation by Church architect Emil Fetzer nearly doubled the temple's 56,062 square feet, added sealing rooms, and replaced the live-acted endowment with the film presentation. President Spencer W. Kimball rededicated the temple that November.
  • The temple closed November 4, 2019, for a four-year renovation: exterior walls reinforced with a two-inch layer of gunite and steel, all mechanical, electrical, and plumbing systems replaced, north and west additions rebuilt to match the original architecture, a bride's exit and an independent baptistry entrance added, and interior finishes returned to 19th-century design patterns.

Symbolism & Design
  • Brigham Young's plan closely followed Joseph Smith's designs for the Nauvoo Temple, carrying that earlier pattern across generations.
  • The red sandstone walls are plastered white, setting the temple apart from the surrounding red rock country.
  • The exterior pairs an octagonal tower and domed cupola with rows of arched and circular windows and white Tuscan columns.
  • The 2019 to 2023 renovation restored the interior to its 1870s and 1880s design period, with new murals by local artists and decorative fixtures matched to designs from a World's Fair catalog.

Trivia
  • It is the only temple completed during Brigham Young's presidency.
  • It was the first temple where the endowment was performed by proxy for the dead. Wilford Woodruff recorded almost 25,000 baptisms for the dead, 12,000 endowments, and 3,800 sealings in the first year alone.
  • A stretch of road between Arizona settlements and St. George was nicknamed "the Honeymoon Trail" because so many couples traveled it to be married in the temple.
  • Almost 670,000 visitors toured the temple during its fall 2023 open house.

Temple facts verified as of August 17, 2026.

Syracuse Utah Temple

Location
Syracuse, Utah. The temple stands on a 12.268-acre site at 1098 South 2500 West, surrounded by farmland between the Great Salt Lake and Interstate 15, about 30 miles northwest of Salt Lake City, at an elevation of 4,275 feet.

Temple Number
The Church's 206th dedicated temple. At its dedication it was the 24th temple dedicated in Utah and the third built in Davis County, following the Bountiful Utah Temple (1995) and the Layton Utah Temple (2024).

Announced
April 5, 2020, by President Russell M. Nelson, in the Sunday afternoon session of a general conference broadcast from Temple Square without a congregation because of the COVID-19 pandemic. It was one of eight temples announced that day, a list that also included Dubai, United Arab Emirates, and Shanghai, People's Republic of China.

Groundbreaking
June 12, 2021. Elder Kevin R. Duncan, General Authority Seventy, presided at the ceremony and offered the site dedicatory prayer.

Dedicated
June 8, 2025, by President Russell M. Nelson, in a single session at 4 p.m., accompanied by Elder Quentin L. Cook of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles. The service was broadcast to meetinghouses throughout the temple district.

Architecture
A three-story steel-frame structure clad in white Moncini granite, with 90,526 square feet of floor area rising 219 feet 8 inches to the top of its single attached end spire.

Ordinance Rooms
Four instruction rooms, four sealing rooms, and two baptistries.

First Temple President
Val Dean Steel, with Luann Kay Flint Steel as matron. Their calls were announced in November 2024, and they began serving at the temple's dedication.

Construction Story
  • The site was announced on August 28, 2020: a 12-acre field at the intersection of 2500 West and 1025 South, still surrounded by working farms. The official exterior rendering followed on February 16, 2021, showing a three-story building of roughly 89,000 square feet.
  • Elder Kevin R. Duncan, who presided at the groundbreaking, grew up on this ground, and his great-grandfather was the first bishop of Syracuse. "I am very familiar with these fields where we stand, where we are gathered today," he said at the ceremony. "From this temple site, I can see the barn roof of my childhood home."
  • The temple was announced in part to ease demand on the Ogden Utah Temple, which was then serving members of 63 stakes. At the announcement, Utah was home to 2.1 million Church members, roughly two-thirds of the state's population.
  • Materials crossed the Atlantic in both directions: the exterior granite was fabricated by Campolonghi of Montignoso, Italy, and installed by IMS Masonry of Lindon, Utah, while the art glass was fabricated by Progetto Arte Poli of Verona, Italy, and installed by Steel Encounters of Salt Lake City.
  • The open house began with a media day on May 7, 2025, followed by tours for invited guests, then a public open house from May 10 to May 31, 2025, excluding Sundays.

Symbolism & Design
  • Design motifs feature the flora of the Great Salt Lake and its nearby wetlands, including the snowball sand-verbena, desert paintbrush, common cattail, and reeds, rendered in shades of blues, greens, golds, yellows, and reds drawn from the area's indigenous plants.
  • The transitioning greens, blues, and yellows in the art glass represent reflections of the lake, a nod to Syracuse's identity as the "Gateway to Antelope Island." The glass features faceted crystal and was designed by Architectural Nexus with assistance from Holdman Studios.
  • Millwork and stain-grade doors are plain sawn sapele, the celestial room carpet is 100 percent New Zealand wool, and the crystal chandeliers were fabricated by Schonbek of Plattsburgh, New York.

Trivia
  • It was the first temple in the Church dedicated with two baptismal fonts. "The reason for that is the high concentration of members and especially high concentration of youth," Elder Kevin R. Duncan explained during the open house. "Now they can come more frequently."
  • Its dedication marked the 200th temple to open its doors during President Russell M. Nelson's 100-year life, and it was the fifth temple he personally dedicated: Sapporo Japan as President of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles, then Concepción Chile, Rome Italy, Deseret Peak Utah, and Syracuse as Church President.
  • The Church's first ward in Syracuse was created on December 1, 1895, nearly 130 years before the city received a temple. The temple's district comprises 16 northern Davis County stakes in Syracuse, West Point, Clearfield, Clinton, and Sunset.
