Whitingham, Vermont

Born Here
Brigham Young, on June 1, 1801. He was the ninth child of John and Abigail Howe Young, who had moved the family up from Hopkinton, Massachusetts, that January.

How Long They Stayed
About three years. Brigham was not quite three when the Youngs left for New York, and he grew up there.

On Town Hill
A 12-foot monument of light Barre granite stands in the town park. Its inscription says it was "erected by descendants of Brigham Young in cooperation with the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints."

What Happened Here
  • January 1801: John and Abigail, called Nabby, brought their children to Whitingham. They were devout Methodists.
  • 1804: The family moved on to Sherburne, in Chenango County, New York.
  • May 28, 1950: President George Albert Smith dedicated the monument on Town Hill before a crowd the Church News put at about 1,000. Four days later, in Washington, he dedicated the Brigham Young statue in the U.S. Capitol, carved by his grandson Mahonri Young.
  • June 1, 2001: For the 200th birthday, about 180 people from around New England met at the small Whitingham Municipal Center in Jacksonville.

On the Map
  1. The traditional birth site is on a hill road west of Town Hill, where a small marker stands in a private front yard. Just where in Whitingham he was born has long been disputed, so the exact spot isn't known; this is the place tradition gives, not a proven one.
  2. The 1950 monument is in the park on Town Hill. Four of Brigham's grandsons drew the original sketch for it.
  3. Jacksonville, the village in the northeast part of town, is home to the Whitingham Municipal Center, where the 2001 birthday program was held.

Trivia
  • The Whitingham circuit was one of the first three Methodist circuits organized in Vermont.
  • A roadside marker on Route 8, described in the Friend in 1971, pointed visitors "southward up the steep hill" to the birthplace.
  • Colonel Nathan Whiting petitioned New York for a township "by the Name of Whitingham," and the patent came through on March 12, 1770. The hill where tradition places his birth has a name of its own now: Brigham's Hill.

Kirtland, Ohio

Why Ohio
A revelation in December 1830 told the Church to "assemble together at the Ohio." It was the first commandment to gather. Late that year Oliver Cowdery and Parley P. Pratt had baptized many members of Sidney Rigdon's congregations near Kirtland.

Headquarters
Kirtland was the Church's headquarters through most of the 1830s, while Joseph Smith and his family lived in Ohio. Dozens of the revelations now in the Doctrine and Covenants were received here.

The Last Company
A group of 515 Saints known as the Kirtland Camp left on July 6, 1838, and reached Adam-ondi-Ahman, Missouri, on October 4.

The Temple Since
A court recognized Joseph Smith's heirs as owners in 1880. About twenty years later the RLDS Church, now Community of Christ, secured title, and it cared for the building until March 5, 2024, when it transferred the temple to The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. Free public tours started on March 25 that year.

What Happened Here
  • Early February 1831: Joseph and Emma Smith arrived at Newel K. Whitney's store, and the Whitneys took them in for about four weeks. On February 4, in that house, Joseph received the revelation calling Edward Partridge as bishop.
  • January 24, 1833: The School of the Prophets first met in an upstairs room of the Whitney store. It ran until about April. Joseph had asked the Lord about the men using tobacco in those meetings, and the Word of Wisdom came on February 27.
  • July 23, 1833: Joseph Smith, Sidney Rigdon and Frederick G. Williams presided as the temple cornerstone was laid. The Saints spent about three years on the building.
  • February 14, 1835: At a meeting honoring the men of Zion's Camp, the Three Witnesses chose the first Quorum of the Twelve Apostles. Eight of the twelve had marched with the camp.
  • March 27, 1836: About a thousand Saints packed the temple for its dedication, with more crowding the doors. Joseph Smith offered a prayer he had received by revelation, now Doctrine and Covenants 109. At a meeting in the temple that evening men spoke in tongues, and Saints outside said they saw a bright cloud and a pillar of fire resting over the building.
  • April 3, 1836: Joseph Smith and Oliver Cowdery lowered the canvas curtains around the top pulpit and knelt to pray. The visions that followed, of the Savior, Moses, Elias and Elijah, are recorded in section 110.
  • January 12, 1838: Joseph Smith and Sidney Rigdon left for Missouri. The Kirtland Safety Society, set up in November 1836, had stopped operating by August 1837 in the Panic of 1837, and some investors, Church leaders among them, had begun to doubt Joseph's prophetic calling.

On the Map
  1. The Whitney store was built in 1826 by Newel K. Whitney and Sidney Gilbert. Over the years it was a post office, the bishop's storehouse and the Church's early headquarters, and Joseph Smith finished his Bible translation there in July 1833. The Whitney home, a few steps away, is the house where Joseph and Emma stayed when they first arrived. Next to it is the Johnson Inn, the first brick building in Kirtland. The Church bought it in 1833, and that December Joseph Smith ordained his father there as patriarch to the Church. It burned in 1915 and was rebuilt on the same spot. Down by the Chagrin River, millwright Joel H. Johnson built the sawmill in six months to cut lumber for the temple, from logs floated down the river. Bishop Whitney's ashery, beside it, turned wood ash into potash for shipping east on the Erie Canal. Both have been rebuilt on their original foundations.
  2. The Isaac and Lucy Morley farm is on Chillicothe Road. Morley had a small house built there for Joseph and Emma, and they lived in it from March to September 1831. Joseph received as many as 13 of the revelations now in the Doctrine and Covenants on the farm, and in its little schoolhouse 23 men, Joseph among them, were ordained high priests. The house standing there now came later and the Smiths' house is gone, so the marker shows the part of the old farm that's open to the public, not the spot where they lived.
  3. The Kirtland Temple is on Chillicothe Road. A short walk up the road is the Joseph and Emma Smith Home. They moved in late in 1833 and stayed just over four years, longer than in any other home they shared. Joseph translated much of the Book of Abraham there, and Emma put together a book of hymns. Kirtland North Cemetery, next to the temple, is older than the Saints' arrival. Joseph's grandmother and Oliver Cowdery's parents are buried in it.
  4. The Stannard Quarry, now part of the Chapin Forest Reservation, supplied stone for the temple's walls. Workmen split the blocks out by hand, drilling holes in the rock and driving in wedges, and for a short time Joseph Smith oversaw the quarrying. Some of the old drill holes are still there by the quarry pond.

Trivia
  • Children gathered broken crockery and china to mix into the exterior stucco. The story that Saints smashed their good dishes for it has no known historical account behind it.
  • The dedicatory prayer, the Hosanna Shout and the W. W. Phelps hymn sung that day all became regular parts of temple dedications afterward.
  • Sidney Rigdon opened the dedication with a sermon that ran more than two hours.

Sharon, Vermont

Which Town
Sharon. Joseph Smith put it plainly in his own history: born "in the town of Sharon, Windsor county, State of Vermont." The memorial's mail goes through South Royalton, the village at the foot of the hill, but the birthplace is in Sharon township.

The Farm
Lucy Mack Smith's father, Solomon Mack, owned it. Joseph Sr. and Lucy rented 68 acres from him and stayed about three years. Joseph Sr. farmed through the growing season and taught school in the winters.

The Monument
A polished granite shaft cut from one stone, 38½ feet long, a foot for each year of Joseph's life. It stands on a 12-foot-square base, and the whole monument is about 50 feet tall. When it went up it was the tallest polished granite shaft in America.

What Happened Here
  • December 23, 1805: Joseph Smith Jr. was born in the family's cabin on the Mack farm.
  • Winter of 1807 to 1808: The Smiths left Sharon for Tunbridge, where Samuel was born that March, and then moved on to Royalton. Joseph, a toddler, probably remembered little of the farm.
  • Autumn 1894: Junius F. Wells came looking for the birthplace with Spencer Clawson and his daughter Clara. A local guide kicked through the tall grass and found the old hearthstone and the stone outline of the cabin. Wells said that someday the Church should put a monument there.
  • 1905: Sent by the First Presidency, Wells traced the old farm boundaries through land titles and the memories of longtime residents, and bought it for the Church. On July 24 he signed the contract for the monument. Granite from Barre came most of the way by rail, and teams hauled each load the last six miles. The first took 13 days, the second 20. The shaft was raised on December 8.
  • December 23, 1905: On the 100th anniversary of the birth, President Joseph F. Smith dedicated the monument. The service was held in a small cottage built over the hearthstone, and the party had come out from Salt Lake City by special train.
  • December 23, 2005: For the bicentennial, President Gordon B. Hinckley spoke from the visitors' center, a couple of feet from the hearthstone. His talk was carried by satellite into the program at the Conference Center and out to meetinghouses across the Church.

On the Map
  1. The Joseph Smith Birthplace Memorial sits on a hilltop east of South Royalton. The obelisk stands on the old farm, and a marker shows where the Smith cabin stood. The cottage of 1905 came down in the 1960s, when the present buildings went up. The original hearthstone is set into the visitors' center fireplace.
  2. South Royalton is the village below the memorial. On the evening of the 1905 dedication, Wells spoke at a meeting there for Church leaders and local residents, and thanked the town for its help.

Trivia
  • The guide who showed Wells the hearthstone in 1894 was named Harvey Smith, a coincidence of names.
  • When 22 horses couldn't budge the first load up the first incline, Wells wrote a telegram asking permission to ship the whole monument to Salt Lake City and put it up on the temple block. He decided to wait until Monday and never sent it.
  • One night a mud hole at the foot of Haines's hill looked impassable. The temperature then fell 35 degrees in about three hours, and by morning the ground was frozen hard enough that the wagons split the planks. People in Royalton took to calling the mild weather that season "Mr. Wells's weather."

History verified as of October 8, 2026.

Palmyra, New York

Canal Town
When the Smith family came in 1816, Palmyra was a village of about 600 people sitting on the planned route of the Erie Canal. The canal opened in 1825 and turned the place into a trading center. The village incorporated two years later, in March 1827.

A Farm Out of Forest
About two miles south of the village, the Smiths made a first payment on 100 acres of thick woods. By the spring of 1820 they had cleared about 30 of them, and they left large stands of timber on the farm's east and west sides.

The First Edition
5,000 copies of a 590-page book, printed and bound in Egbert B. Grandin's shop on Main Street by about a dozen men over seven months. An ordinary book of the day was printed in runs of less than half that.

What Happened Here
  • 1817: The Smiths rented a house in the village for about two years. Joseph Sr., Alvin and Hyrum hired out as day laborers, the family ran a small shop, and Lucy painted oilcloth covers for tables and chests while they saved toward land of their own.
  • Spring 1820: Joseph, 14, went into the woods near the house to pray, probably close to ground the family was clearing. He later wrote that it was the first time he had tried to pray out loud. There, by his account, God the Father and Jesus Christ appeared to him.
  • September 21, 1823: In the middle of harvest, the angel Moroni came to Joseph three times in the night, in a bedroom of the log home he shared with his brothers. By the third visit it was nearly dawn.
  • September 1827: Joseph and Emma were living in the family's frame house when he brought the plates home. He hid them under the hearth bricks, then in the loft of the cooper's shop with the empty box buried under the floor. A mob tore up the floorboards and smashed the box, and never looked in the loft overhead.
  • June 1829: Grandin turned the printing job down, believing the book was a fraud. Joseph Smith and Martin Harris found a printer in Rochester willing to take it, then came back and asked Grandin again. This time he agreed to print and bind 5,000 copies for $3,000. On August 25 Harris, a Palmyra farmer, mortgaged his farm north of the village to Grandin to secure the bill.
  • March 26, 1830: The first copies went on sale in Grandin's bookstore, bound in brown calfskin with "Book of Mormon" in gold on the spine.

On the Map
  1. The Erie Canal still runs through the village, a few hundred yards north of Main Street.
  2. The Smith farm is on Stafford Road. The Church bought it in 1907. The log home was rebuilt on its original foundation and dedicated in 1998, and the frame house, about 125 yards south, has been restored along with the barn and the cooper's shop.
  3. The Sacred Grove lies west of the houses, across the farm, with paths through it. No one can place the First Vision any closer than the wooded part of the farm, so the marker stands for the grove, not a known spot. The old forest there has gone by the name Sacred Grove since at least 1905.
  4. Hill Cumorah, in Manchester about three miles south of the farm, is where Joseph went the day after Moroni's visits in 1823. He brought the plates home from it in September 1827. The Angel Moroni Monument on its summit was dedicated in 1935. Joseph put the plates on the hill's west side, not far from the top, and no source pins the spot down more closely than that.
  5. The Grandin building stands at 217 East Main Street. The Church was given it in 1978, and after two and a half years of restoration President Gordon B. Hinckley dedicated it on March 26, 1998, 168 years to the day after the first copies went on sale. A few hundred yards away, in the old cemetery on Church Street, is the grave of Alvin Smith, Joseph's oldest brother. He died in November 1823 at 25.
  6. The Martin Harris farm, the one he mortgaged to Grandin, is on Maple Avenue north of the village. Willard Bean bought 88 acres of it for the Church in 1937. The cobblestone house on it now stands where the original farmhouse did.
  7. The Palmyra New York Temple sits on a drumlin on the east side of the old farm. President Hinckley dedicated it on April 6, 2000. Its grounds are edged by a rock wall Joseph and his brothers piled up while clearing fields.

Trivia
  • The farm had as many as 1,500 maple trees, and each spring the Smiths turned the sap into sugar and molasses.
  • Loose printed sheets left Grandin's shop before the book did. Thomas B. Marsh was handed 16 pages and took them home to Boston, and Solomon Chamberlin got 64 and carried them on to Canada.
  • Harris's August mortgage gave him 18 months to pay. Grandin didn't wait. In October 1830 he sold the mortgage for $2,000 in cash, and its new holder collected the full $3,000 when Harris's land was sold in April 1831.

Which Town
Sharon. Joseph Smith put it plainly in his own history: born "in the town of Sharon, Windsor county, State of Vermont." The memorial's mail goes through South Royalton, the village at the foot of the hill, but the birthplace is in Sharon township.

Lucy Mack Smith's father, Solomon Mack, owned it. Joseph Sr. and Lucy rented 68 acres from him and stayed about three years. Joseph Sr. farmed through the growing season and taught school in the winters.

  • December 23, 1805: Joseph Smith Jr. was born in the family's cabin on the Mack farm.
  • Winter of 1807 to 1808: The Smiths left Sharon for Tunbridge, where Samuel was born that March, and then moved on to Royalton. Joseph, a toddler, probably remembered little of the farm.
  • Autumn 1894: Junius F. Wells came looking for the birthplace with Spencer Clawson and his daughter Clara. A local guide kicked through the tall grass and found the old hearthstone and the stone outline of the cabin. Wells said that someday the Church should put a monument there.

On July 24 he signed the contract for the monument. Granite from Barre came most of the way by rail, and teams hauled each load the last six miles. The first took 13 days, the second 20.   • December 23, 2005: For the bicentennial, President Gordon B. Hinckley spoke from the visitors' center, a couple of feet from the hearthstone. His talk was carried by satellite into the program at the Conference Center and out to meetinghouses across the Church.

  1. The Joseph Smith Birthplace Memorial sits on a hilltop east of South Royalton. The obelisk stands on the old farm, and a marker shows where the Smith cabin stood.   2. South Royalton is the village below the memorial. On the evening of the 1905 dedication, Wells spoke at a meeting there for Church leaders and local residents, and thanked the town for its help.

  • The guide who showed Wells the hearthstone in 1894 was named Harvey Smith, a coincidence of names.

  • One night a mud hole at the foot of Haines's hill looked impassable. The temperature then fell 35 degrees in about three hours, and by morning the ground was frozen hard enough that the wagons split the planks.   • September 22, 1823: The day after Moroni's visits, Joseph went to the hill, pried up a stone with a lever, and found the plates in a box of stones set in cement. He was not allowed to take them, and was told to come back on the same day each year.
  • September 22, 1827: After four years of meeting the angel there, Joseph took the plates from the hill.
  • Early 1928: The Church owned only a farm partway up the west slope, bought in 1923, when the lawyer for the estate of the banker Pliny T. Sexton called the Church's agent, Willard Bean, to his office. Bean came away with the rest of the hill, three farms beside it and the Grange Hall, for $53,000.
  • 1930s: Willard and Rebecca Bean planted 65,000 evergreens from the state conservation department on a hilltop farmers had cleared almost bare, plus 3,000 seedlings dug up near the Sacred Grove.
  • 1935: President Heber J. Grant dedicated the Angel Moroni Monument on the summit, the work of sculptor Torleif Knaphus.
  • September 21, 2025: Elder David A. Bednar rededicated the site, 202 years to the day after Moroni first came to Joseph. Since 2021 crews had taken out 23 pageant buildings and more than nine acres of asphalt and gravel and started the hill back toward forest.

  1. The Smith farm on Stafford Road has both of the family's houses. The restored frame house is the one on the Manchester side. The log home, rebuilt on its original foundation, is about 125 yards north, across the town line in Palmyra.

Joseph Smith said God the Father and Jesus Christ appeared to him in the woods near his home in the spring of 1820, but nobody can place it more exactly than the wooded part of the farm.   • Manchester didn't exist under that name when the Smiths arrived. The town was split off from Farmington as Burt in March 1821 and renamed Manchester in April 1822.
  • Sexton once asked $100,000 for the hill. Bean told him the Church had done fine without it for nearly a century and could keep waiting.
  • The last Hill Cumorah Pageant was performed in July 2019, not 2020. The Church had announced 2020 as the final season, the pandemic pushed that to 2021, and in March 2021 it was called off for good.

Colesville, New York

The Township
Colesville split off from Windsor in 1821 and had about 2,400 people by 1830. Harpursville, Nineveh and Colesville were its villages, and the Susquehanna River ran through its eastern side.

Joseph Knight Sr.
A farmer and miller who moved his family in 1811 to the part of Windsor that later became Colesville. He hired Joseph Smith as a day laborer in 1826, and later, while the Book of Mormon was being translated in Harmony, he brought Joseph food and paper.

The Branch
The Knights and their neighbors became one of the Church's first branches, possibly the very first. Hyrum Smith presided over it for several months from late 1830. Newel Knight, Joseph Sr.'s son, led it after him.

What Happened Here
  • April 1830: Days after the Church was organized, Joseph stopped at the Knight farm and preached to the family and their friends. Newel Knight came back from praying alone in the woods seized by a fit. Joseph commanded the devil, in the name of Jesus Christ, to depart from him, and the fit stopped. Joseph called it the first miracle performed in the Church.
  • June 28, 1830: Joseph and others had dammed a stream for a baptism, and someone tore the dam out overnight. Early on the 28th the believers rebuilt it, and Oliver Cowdery baptized thirteen people in the pool, Emma Smith and Joseph and Polly Knight among them. Men on the bank jeered, then followed the group back to the Knight house, where they grew into a crowd of about fifty.
  • June 30, 1830: Arrested that evening and acquitted in Chenango County the next day, Joseph was arrested again by a Broome County constable and held overnight at a Colesville tavern. Justice Joel K. Noble and at least two other justices heard the case and discharged him.
  • April 1831: Told by revelation to gather to Ohio, the branch sold what it could and set out together, poor families included. In Ohio they were sent to Leman Copley's 759-acre farm in Thompson. Copley soon went back on his offer and evicted them.
  • July 26, 1831: About sixty branch members reached Kaw Township in Jackson County, Missouri, roughly a thousand miles from Thompson. On August 2, Joseph and twelve men of the branch laid the first log of the first house in Zion. Within the week Polly Knight had died, the first Church member to die in Zion.

  1. Nineveh is probably where Joseph worked for Joseph Knight Sr. in 1826 and 1827. Sources say only that the work was likely near Nineveh, so the marker shows the hamlet, not a known farm or building.

  3. Nathaniel Cole's tavern stood near where Colesville Road now meets Watrous Road, and pieces of its foundation remain. BYU historians call it the probable place of Joseph's June 30, 1830 trial. Church sources say only "a Colesville tavern," so this spot isn't certain.

Trivia
  • Joseph Knight considered Joseph Smith "the best hand he ever hired."
  • When snow made the road to Harmony hard going, Joseph sometimes borrowed the Knights' sleigh to go courting Emma.

Phinehas Young read the Book of Mormon he bought at the Tomlinson Inn, then passed it to his father and to his sister Fanny. Fanny gave it to Brigham.

  • Spring 1832: The Mendon Branch was organized with about 30 members. Eleven were Youngs. They met in an upstairs room at the Tomlinson Inn.
  • September 8, 1832: Miriam Young died of tuberculosis. Brigham buried her in the Tomlinson Corners cemetery, then moved with his two daughters into Heber and Vilate Kimball's house for about a year and a half.

  1. John Young's farm took in the corners where Cheese Factory Road meets the Mendon-Ionia Road. At the back of the property Brigham built his own house over the creek, the same little mill stream he was baptized in: the mill downstairs, the family upstairs. After the Youngs left, later owners tore the mill down and left the pieces in the stream. Sheldon Fisher dug there for six summers and found silverware, tools and parts of the house.   • Heber C. Kimball later recalled women walking three miles from Victor to meetings in Mendon.
  • Fisher's dig also turned up pottery made by Heber C. Kimball.
  • Brigham built a house for his father on the road south of the village. It was later split in two and half of it moved across Cheese Factory Road. Both halves still stand there facing each other, each one enlarged into a house of its own.

Newel Knight came back from praying alone in the woods seized by a fit. Joseph commanded the devil, in the name of Jesus Christ, to depart from him, and the fit stopped. Men on the bank jeered, then followed the group back to the Knight house, where they grew into a crowd of about fifty.
  • June 30, 1830: Arrested that evening and acquitted in Chenango County the next day, Joseph was arrested again by a Broome County constable and held overnight at a Colesville tavern. Justice Joel K. Noble and at least two other justices heard the case and discharged him.
  • April 1831: Told by revelation to gather to Ohio, the branch sold what it could and set out together, poor families included. In Ohio they were sent to Leman Copley's 759-acre farm in Thompson. Copley soon went back on his offer and evicted them.
  • July 26, 1831: About sixty branch members reached Kaw Township in Jackson County, Missouri, roughly a thousand miles from Thompson. Mendon, New York

Neighbors
The Youngs and the Kimballs. Brigham Young's father, John, came to Mendon in 1827, and Brigham moved his own family onto his father's farm in the spring of 1829. Heber C. Kimball, a blacksmith and potter, had married Vilate Murray here in 1822.

A Book Passed Hand to Hand
Phinehas Young read the Book of Mormon he bought at the Tomlinson Inn, then passed it to his father and to his sister Fanny. Fanny gave it to Brigham.

Leaving
The Youngs and Kimballs moved to Kirtland, Ohio, in 1833. By that September the inn's part in Church history was over.

What Happened Here
  • April 1830: At the Tomlinson Inn, Samuel Smith, the Prophet's brother, sold a copy of the new Book of Mormon to Phinehas Young, Brigham's brother.
  • Sunday, April 15, 1832: Eleazer Miller baptized Brigham Young. Brigham remembered it as "in my own little mill stream," and Miller confirmed him at the water's edge. Heber C. Kimball was baptized by Alpheus Gifford the same week, and Brigham's wife, Miriam, about three weeks later.
  • Spring 1832: The Mendon Branch was organized with about 30 members. Eleven were Youngs. They met in an upstairs room at the Tomlinson Inn.
  • September 8, 1832: Miriam Young died of tuberculosis. Brigham buried her in the Tomlinson Corners cemetery, then moved with his two daughters into Heber and Vilate Kimball's house for about a year and a half.

On the Map
  1. John Young's farm took in the corners where Cheese Factory Road meets the Mendon-Ionia Road. At the back of the property Brigham built his own house over the creek, the same little mill stream he was baptized in: the mill downstairs, the family upstairs. After the Youngs left, later owners tore the mill down and left the pieces in the stream. Sheldon Fisher dug there for six summers and found silverware, tools and parts of the house. He later sold a van full of Brigham's belongings to the Museum of Church History and Art in Salt Lake City. Sources don't say where on the farm the mill stood, so the marker is at the corners.
  2. Tomlinson Corners, south of Mendon village on the Mendon-Ionia Road. The inn stood a short way down the road from the little graveyard where Miriam is buried. No source gives the inn's exact site; the marker is at the graveyard.

Trivia
  • Heber C. Kimball later recalled women walking three miles from Victor to meetings in Mendon.
  • Fisher's dig also turned up pottery made by Heber C. Kimball.
  • Brigham built a house for his father on the road south of the village. It was later split in two and half of it moved across Cheese Factory Road. Both halves still stand there facing each other, each one enlarged into a house of its own.

History verified as of October 9, 2026.

- Evan

Harmony, Pennsylvania

On Today's Maps
Oakland Township, Susquehanna County. Harmony village no longer exists, and it shouldn't be mixed up with the Harmony near Pittsburgh, across the state.

Emma's Family
Emma Hale was born in what became Harmony on July 10, 1804, the seventh of Isaac and Elizabeth Hale's nine children. Isaac farmed, hunted and kept an inn, and shipped meat downriver to Philadelphia and Baltimore. In late 1825 Josiah Stowell's crew of silver diggers boarded at the Hale place, Joseph Smith among them.

Scripture From Here
Most of the Book of Mormon was translated in Harmony, and 15 sections of the Doctrine and Covenants were received here.

What Happened Here
  • December 1827: Joseph and Emma arrived from Manchester, New York, with the plates. In February 1828 they moved into a small house on a lot next to her parents' land.
  • June 15, 1828: Martin Harris had been Joseph's scribe since April, and by mid-June the manuscript ran to at least 116 pages. Harris took it home to show his family. The day after he left, Emma gave birth to a son who died soon after, and she nearly died herself. Joseph went north to find Harris and learned the pages were lost. Back in Harmony that July, he received the revelation now in section 3.
  • April 7, 1829: Oliver Cowdery, a schoolteacher who had boarded with Joseph's parents, arrived on foot on April 5 with Joseph's brother Samuel. Two days later he started writing as Joseph dictated, and the pages piled up at six to eight a day.
  • May 15, 1829: Joseph and Oliver went into the woods to pray about baptism. John the Baptist appeared and conferred the Aaronic Priesthood on them, and they baptized each other in the Susquehanna.
  • August 26, 1830: Joseph paid Isaac Hale the last of what he owed for the farm. Soon after, he and Emma left for Fayette, New York. Emma never saw her parents again.
  • September 19, 2015: President Russell M. Nelson, then President of the Quorum of the Twelve, dedicated the renovated Priesthood Restoration Site after three years of work. The state highway that had split the two homes was rerouted first, with the Church's help.

On the Map
  1. The Joseph and Emma Smith Home and the Isaac and Elizabeth Hale Home are reconstructions, built on the footprints of the originals. The old foundation stones now face the Hale home's foundation and make up a fence around the Smith home. A short walk away, McKune Cemetery holds Joseph and Emma's first child and Emma's parents. Next to it is the Aaronic Priesthood monument the Church put up in 1960, sculpted by Avard Fairbanks.
  2. A trail runs into the sugar maple grove, or sugar bush, beside the visitors' center, where the Aaronic Priesthood was most likely restored. Joseph's history says only that they went into the woods. The exact spot isn't known; the marker shows the grove historians point to.
  3. Another trail goes down to the bank of the Susquehanna where Joseph and Oliver were baptized. Sources don't say exactly where along the river they waded in; the marker shows where the trail meets the bank.

Trivia
  • For years the John the Baptist scene was pictured on the riverbank, a habit that traces back to an early painting. Historians now place it in the maple grove.
  • Oliver later wrote that on Monday, his first full day in Harmony, he helped Joseph with "some business of a temporal nature." It was the agreement to buy the house, barn and land from Isaac Hale for $200, with $64 down, written out in Oliver's hand and witnessed by him and Samuel. The date on it is April 6, 1829, one year to the day before the Church was organized.

History verified as of October 9, 2026.

- Evan

Afton, New York

Then Called
South Bainbridge, a village in the town of Bainbridge, Chenango County. Joseph Smith's own history uses that name for where he married Emma Hale.

Josiah Stowell
Born in New Hampshire in 1770, he settled in the town in 1791, farmed, and owned a sawmill. His house stood near the Susquehanna, just southwest of the village. He hired Joseph in 1825 and stood by him in court twice.

What Survives
Not much on paper from 1826. The justice's docket book and the case papers from Joseph's first hearing are lost, and what remains comes from later printings. Even the outcome is uncertain.

What Happened Here
  • November 1825: Joseph and his father signed on with Stowell to dig for a Spanish silver mine rumored to lie near Harmony, Pennsylvania. After nearly a month Joseph talked him out of it. He stayed on to work Stowell's farm here, 28 miles from Emma's home.
  • March 20, 1826: Joseph went before Albert Neely, a justice of the peace in Bainbridge, on a disorderly person charge. The published docket names Stowell's nephew Peter Bridgman as the complainant. Stowell told the court Joseph had not swindled him. The record names Bainbridge and stops there, so which village heard the case is still open.
  • January 18, 1827: Emma was visiting the Stowells when Joseph proposed. Her parents opposed the match, so the two were married "at the house of Squire Tarbill, in South Bainbridge," as Joseph put it. Stowell then helped them move to Manchester to live with Joseph's parents.
  • June 29, 1830: Arrested in Colesville the evening before, Joseph was brought here by Constable Ebenezer Hatch and kept overnight at a tavern. Justice Joseph Chamberlin heard twelve witnesses, Stowell among them, and Joseph was acquitted.

On the Map
  1. The Josiah Stowell Home is on State Route 7 southwest of the village. The Church doesn't own or run it, and docents give tours.
  2. The Tarbill house stood where the Afton Fair grounds are now. The house is gone, but a roadside marker shows the spot. For years the sign called the bride "Emily Hale." The newer one gets her name right.
  3. The Joseph Knight Sr. Home, over the county line in Colesville, is where Constable Hatch arrested Joseph on the evening of June 28, 1830.
  4. South Bainbridge, the village now called Afton, is where Joseph spent that night at a tavern and was tried the next day. Which tavern, and which building held the trial, isn't known, so the marker shows the village center. Where the 1826 hearing met is not known either; its record says only Bainbridge, which then named the whole town.

Trivia
  • Joseph's two defenders in 1830, James Davidson and John S. Reed, were farmers, not lawyers.
  • The ground here was called Jericho when Stowell arrived. The town became Bainbridge in 1814, and in 1857 South Bainbridge broke off as its own town and took the name Afton, after Afton Water, the Ayrshire stream Robert Burns wrote about in "Flow gently, sweet Afton."

History verified as of October 9, 2026.

Afton, New York

Then Called
South Bainbridge, a village in the town of Bainbridge, Chenango County. Joseph Smith's own history uses that name for where he married Emma Hale.

Josiah Stowell
Born in New Hampshire in 1770, he settled in the town in 1791, farmed, and owned a sawmill. His house stood near the Susquehanna, just southwest of the village. He hired Joseph in 1825 and stood by him in court twice.

What Survives
Not much on paper from 1826. The justice's docket book and the case papers from Joseph's first hearing are lost, and what remains comes from later printings. Even the outcome is uncertain.

What Happened Here
  • November 1825: Joseph and his father signed on with Stowell to dig for a Spanish silver mine rumored to lie near Harmony, Pennsylvania. After nearly a month Joseph talked him out of it. He stayed on to work Stowell's farm here, 28 miles from Emma's home.
  • March 20, 1826: Joseph went before Albert Neely, a justice of the peace in Bainbridge, on a disorderly person charge. The published docket names Stowell's nephew Peter Bridgman as the complainant. Stowell told the court Joseph had not swindled him. The record names Bainbridge and stops there, so which village heard the case is still open.
  • January 18, 1827: Emma was visiting the Stowells when Joseph proposed. Her parents opposed the match, so the two were married "at the house of Squire Tarbill, in South Bainbridge," as Joseph put it. Stowell then helped them move to Manchester to live with Joseph's parents.
  • June 29, 1830: Arrested in Colesville the evening before, Joseph was brought here by Constable Ebenezer Hatch and kept overnight at a tavern. Justice Joseph Chamberlin heard twelve witnesses, Stowell among them, and Joseph was acquitted.

On the Map
  1. The Josiah Stowell Home is on State Route 7 southwest of the village. The Church doesn't own or run it, and docents give tours.
  2. The Tarbill house stood where the Afton Fair grounds are now. The house is gone, but a roadside marker shows the spot. For years the sign called the bride "Emily Hale." The newer one gets her name right.
  3. The Joseph Knight Sr. Home, over the county line in Colesville, is where Constable Hatch arrested Joseph on the evening of June 28, 1830.
  4. South Bainbridge, the village now called Afton, is where Joseph spent that night at a tavern and was tried the next day. Which tavern, and which building held the trial, isn't known, so the marker shows the village center. Where the 1826 hearing met is not known either; its record says only Bainbridge, which then named the whole town.

Trivia
  • Joseph's two defenders in 1830, James Davidson and John S. Reed, were farmers, not lawyers.
  • The ground here was called Jericho when Stowell arrived. The town became Bainbridge in 1814, and in 1857 South Bainbridge broke off as its own town and took the name Afton, after Afton Water, the Ayrshire stream Robert Burns wrote about in "Flow gently, sweet Afton."

- Evan

Hiram, Ohio

The Johnsons
John and Elsa Johnson came from Vermont in 1818 and built up a big farm with fields, pasture and a dairy. Their son Lyman joined the Church in February 1831. John and Elsa read the Book of Mormon with their minister, went to Kirtland to meet Joseph Smith, and Elsa came home with her rheumatic arm healed. They were baptized soon after.

The House
Two stories and five bedrooms, built in 1828. When it went up it was one of the finest houses in the area.

Why Joseph Came
He wanted a quiet place to get on with his revision of the Bible. Through the winter he and Sidney Rigdon, his scribe, worked in an upstairs room, and much of what Joseph received in Hiram grew out of that work.

What Happened Here
  • September 12, 1831: Joseph and Emma moved in with their adopted twins, Joseph and Julia, four months old. Sidney and Phebe Rigdon and their six children took a log cabin across the road.
  • November 1 to 12, 1831: Elders met at the house in four special conferences and voted to publish Joseph's revelations as the Book of Commandments. The conference called them "worth to the Church the riches of the whole Earth." The Lord's preface to the book, now Doctrine and Covenants 1, came on the first day.
  • December 1, 1831: A revelation set the Bible work aside and sent Joseph and Sidney out to preach, to answer letters Ezra Booth had published in a local paper. On January 10, 1832, another told them to go back to translating.
  • February 16, 1832: With about twelve men in the upstairs room, Joseph and Sidney saw the vision of the kingdoms of glory, now Doctrine and Covenants 76. It came while they were working on John 5:29, about the resurrection of the just and the unjust.
  • March 24, 1832: A mob of local militiamen broke into the house at night, dragged Joseph from his bed, and tarred and feathered him and Sidney in a meadow some distance from the house. Emma and Elsa Johnson worked through the night to clean off the tar. The next day Joseph preached as usual and baptized three people. Both twins had measles. The boy, Joseph, died later that week.
  • September 12, 1832: The Smiths moved back to Kirtland, a year to the day after they came. In the spring of 1834 John Johnson sold most of his land, gave $3,000 to the Church, and moved the family to Kirtland, where they ran an inn near the Whitney store.

On the Map
  1. The John and Elsa Johnson Home stands on Pioneer Trail. Joseph preached from its front steps to people standing in the yard. The Church restored it to its original look, and President Gordon B. Hinckley dedicated it on October 28, 2001. That service was held at the Hiram Ward meetinghouse, just west of the farm, an alfalfa field away.

Trivia
  • Some elders at the November conference questioned the "imperfections" in the revelations' language. A revelation given there, now section 67, challenged the wisest of them to write one as good as the least of Joseph's.
  • When the 1832 vision closed, Sidney looked limp and pale. Joseph smiled and said, "Sidney is not used to it as I am."
  • The handwritten book the conference approved, now called Revelation Book 1, left Hiram with Oliver Cowdery and John Whitmer in November 1831 and reached Independence in January. There they and the printer, William W. Phelps, marked corrections and verse numbers straight onto its pages and set the Book of Commandments from it. Later it went back to Ohio and served as printer's copy a second time, for the 1835 Doctrine and Covenants.

Two stories and five bedrooms, built in 1828. When it went up it was one of the finest houses in the area.

  • December 1, 1831: A revelation set the Bible work aside and sent Joseph and Sidney out to preach, to answer letters Ezra Booth had published in a local paper. On January 10, 1832, another told them to go back to translating.

Liberty, Missouri

Clay County Seat
Settled in 1820 and named county seat in 1822. After the Saints were driven out of Jackson County in 1833, many of them found refuge here in Clay County.

The Prisoners
Joseph Smith, Hyrum Smith, Sidney Rigdon, Lyman Wight, Caleb Baldwin and Alexander McRae, sent from the Richmond hearing to wait for trial on treason. They were held from December 1, 1838, to April 6, 1839, a little over four months.

In Joseph's Words
From a letter of March 22, 1839: "We are kept under a strong guard, night and day, … our food is scant, uniform, and coarse; we have not the privilege of cooking for ourselves, we have been compelled to sleep on the floor with straw, and not blankets sufficient to keep us warm; and when we have a fire, we are obliged to have almost a constant smoke."

What Happened Here
  • December 1, 1838: After a day in a wagon from Richmond, the six men were taken north past the courthouse to the small stone jail. A crowd pressed in to watch. Joseph was the last one off the wagon, and at the door he raised his hat to the crowd before going down into the lower room.
  • February 1839: Hyrum's wife, Mary Fielding Smith, came with their baby, Joseph F. Smith, born the November before. It was the first time Hyrum had seen his son. That same month Sidney Rigdon, gravely ill, was released on bail. Emma Smith came three times over the winter, once bringing young Joseph III.
  • March 20, 1839: The day after letters came from Emma, Don Carlos Smith and Bishop Edward Partridge, Joseph began dictating two long letters to the Church. The second followed around March 22. Parts of them are now Doctrine and Covenants 121, 122 and 123, and section 121 opens with Joseph's prayer, "O God, where art thou?" The first letter runs seventeen pages, in the handwriting of Alexander McRae and Caleb Baldwin.
  • April 6, 1839: An armed guard took the prisoners out of the jail to face a grand jury in Gallatin. They won a change of venue to Boone County, and on the way there the guards let them escape. They made it to Illinois.

On the Map
  1. South of town on Campbell Drive, on what was Michael Arthur's farm, a granite monument to the Eight Witnesses stands near the graves of two of them, Christian Whitmer and Peter Whitmer Jr. In the mid-1830s the farm served as a gathering place for Church leaders, and Joseph Smith organized the first Missouri presidency there in July 1834. The monument was dedicated on November 19, 2011.
  2. The Historic Liberty Jail is on North Main Street. The old jail fell into disrepair after 1856, and on June 19, 1939, Wilford C. Wood bought the site and passed it to the Church. Today a visitors' center there holds a full-scale reconstruction of the jail, with stairs down from the rotunda for a closer look. Joseph Fielding Smith dedicated the site on September 15, 1963. A few hundred feet south is the site of Alexander W. Doniphan's 1830s home, marked in 2002. Doniphan, a Liberty lawyer, defended Joseph and the others in court.

Trivia
  • Wilford Wood paid $4,000 for the jail site in 1939 and sold it to the Church for exactly what he paid.
  • The jail was 14 by 14½ feet and two stories high. Its walls had three layers: rough limestone two feet thick outside, oak inside, and a one-foot gap between them packed with loose rock to discourage escapes. The only way into the lower room was a trapdoor from the upper floor, and its two barred windows were each 2 feet wide and 6 inches high.

Adam-ondi-Ahman, Missouri

In Scripture
Section 107, recorded in 1835, says that three years before he died Adam called his righteous posterity "into the valley of Adam-ondi-Ahman" and gave them his last blessing. Section 116, given at Spring Hill in May or June 1838, reads: "Spring Hill is named by the Lord Adam-ondi-Ahman, because, said he, it is the place where Adam shall come to visit his people, or the Ancient of Days shall sit, as spoken of by Daniel the prophet."

Back in Church Hands
The Church announced the purchase of Spring Hill in March 1944. The final deeds were dated June 27, 1944, a hundred years to the day after Joseph and Hyrum Smith were killed. The seller, Eugene Johnson, came from a family that had held the land for a century.

What Happened Here
  • Early 1838: A few Latter-day Saint families settled below the bluffs along the Grand River in Daviess County and called the place Spring Hill, for the springs running off the bluff. Lyman and Harriet Wight built one of the first homes, and Lyman ran a ferry across the river.
  • May 19, 1838: Joseph Smith and a party of Church leaders rode up the river to Wight's. Joseph wrote of grass-covered prairie and "plenty of wild game in this land, such as deer, turkey, hens, elk." They surveyed a city on the bluffs, and the revelation naming Adam-ondi-Ahman followed.
  • June 28, 1838: Joseph Smith organized a stake here, the Church's third, with his uncle John Smith as president and Lyman Wight and Reynolds Cahoon as counselors. The survey ran to more than 520 blocks over four square miles, and more than 200 homes went up that summer and fall.
  • November 1838: Early in the month Missouri militiamen ordered every Latter-day Saint out of the county, under the governor's extermination order. By November 20 the town was nearly empty. Lyman Wight was arrested and spent five months jailed with Joseph Smith at Liberty.

On the Map
  1. The Wight home site sits at the foot of Tower Hill, where Joseph Smith found Lyman Wight living in 1838. A half-mile round-trip trail climbs to it. The two-story log house is gone, but its spot is marked.
  2. Spring Hill Summit, the high bluff the revelation named, has only a simple sign. It looks down on the valley and a bend of the Grand River.
  3. The Valley Overlook, a short walk southeast of its parking lot, takes in the valley between Spring Hill and the river.

Trivia
  • Residents called the town Diahman for short.
  • Tower Hill got its name from a stack of rocks the settlers took for the ruins of an old tower.
  • Senior missionaries look after the trails and overlooks, which are open daily from dawn to dusk. Much of the Church's land around them is farmed.

Liberty, Missouri

Clay County Seat
Settled in 1820 and named county seat in 1822. After the Saints were driven out of Jackson County in 1833, many of them found refuge here in Clay County.

The Prisoners
Joseph Smith, Hyrum Smith, Sidney Rigdon, Lyman Wight, Caleb Baldwin and Alexander McRae, sent from the Richmond hearing to wait for trial on treason. They were held from December 1, 1838, to April 6, 1839, a little over four months.

In Joseph's Words
From a letter of March 22, 1839: "We are kept under a strong guard, night and day, … our food is scant, uniform, and coarse; we have not the privilege of cooking for ourselves, we have been compelled to sleep on the floor with straw, and not blankets sufficient to keep us warm; and when we have a fire, we are obliged to have almost a constant smoke."

  • December 1, 1838: After a day in a wagon from Richmond, the six men were taken north past the courthouse to the small stone jail. A crowd pressed in to watch. Joseph was the last one off the wagon, and at the door he raised his hat to the crowd before going down into the lower room.
  • February 1839: Hyrum's wife, Mary Fielding Smith, came with their baby, Joseph F. Smith, born the November before. It was the first time Hyrum had seen his son.   • March 20, 1839: The day after letters came from Emma, Don Carlos Smith and Bishop Edward Partridge, Joseph began dictating two long letters to the Church. The second followed around March 22.   1.   • May 19, 1838: Joseph Smith and a party of Church leaders rode up the river to Wight's. Joseph wrote of grass-covered prairie and "plenty of wild game in this land, such as deer, turkey, hens, elk." They surveyed a city on the bluffs, and the revelation naming Adam-ondi-Ahman followed.
  • June 28, 1838: Joseph Smith organized a stake here, the Church's third, with his uncle John Smith as president and Lyman Wight and Reynolds Cahoon as counselors. The survey ran to more than 520 blocks over four square miles, and more than 200 homes went up that summer and fall.

  1. The Wight home site sits at the foot of Tower Hill, where Joseph Smith found Lyman Wight living in 1838. A half-mile round-trip trail climbs to it. The two-story log house is gone, but its spot is marked.
  2. Spring Hill Summit, the high bluff the revelation named, has only a simple sign. It looks down on the valley and a bend of the Grand River.
  3. The Valley Overlook, a short walk southeast of its parking lot, takes in the valley between Spring Hill and the river.

Trivia
  • Residents called the town Diahman for short.
  • Tower Hill got its name from a stack of rocks the settlers took for the ruins of an old tower.
  • Senior missionaries look after the trails and overlooks, which are open daily from dawn to dusk. Much of the Church's land around them is farmed.

That's why I started this company. It doesn't take much for someone who has been prepared to tap you on the shoulder and ask a question that changes the direction of their life. No argument, no pitch, no lesson plan. Just an opening.

- Evan

Quincy, Illinois

The Town
Settled in 1821 on limestone bluffs above the Mississippi, and the Adams County seat from 1825. In the winter of 1838 to 1839 it had about 1,500 people by one Church count and 1,600 by another.

The Exiles
More than 5,000 Latter-day Saints driven out of Missouri came to Quincy that winter. Thousands walked east across the frozen river. Townspeople took families into their homes, found them work, and gathered food, clothing and money.

Upriver
Quincy was a stopping place. Within about a year most of the Saints had moved some 45 miles north to Commerce, which became Nauvoo.

What Happened Here
  • Mid-February 1839: Emma Smith, with Joseph still jailed in Missouri, crossed the frozen Mississippi on foot with her four children. Under her skirt, in cotton bags a friend had sewn, she carried the manuscripts of Joseph's Bible translation. She found lodging with Judge John Cleveland and his wife, Sarah, about four miles from town.
  • February 25 to 28, 1839: The Democratic Association of Quincy met over several days, named a relief committee chaired by J. W. Whitney, and passed resolutions condemning Missouri's treatment of the Saints. The committee set out to feed, clothe and house at least 5,000 people.
  • April 22, 1839: Joseph Smith stepped off a ferry at Quincy after escaping custody in Missouri, in a wide-brimmed hat with his collar turned up. Dimick Huntington recognized him on the bank and took him by back streets to the Cleveland place, where Emma ran out and met him halfway to the gate.
  • May 4 to 6, 1839: A general conference at a Presbyterian camp ground just outside town approved the land purchases at Commerce and the Twelve's mission to Europe. Joseph and his family left for Commerce on May 10.
  • June 28, 2002: In the area for the Nauvoo Temple dedication, President Gordon B. Hinckley and the Tabernacle Choir gave Quincy a benefit concert. It raised $75,000 to help the city start a community foundation.

On the Map
  1. Washington Park, on Maine Street between 4th and 5th, holds a marker the Church and the Illinois State Historical Society placed in 1976. It says many of the Saints who crossed into Illinois at Quincy "were made welcome by the people here."
  2. Clat Adams Bicentennial Park sits on the riverfront. In May 2025, for the county's 200th anniversary, the Church unveiled a rendering of its "Mercy on the Mississippi" panel for the park. Its background painting shows Saints huddled on the shore, waiting to cross the icy river.

Trivia
  • Eliza R. Snow's poem "To the Citizens of Quincy" ran in the Quincy Whig on May 11, 1839, addressed to the town's "Sons and Daughters of Benevolence."
  • Quincy got its own stake on October 25, 1840. It was cut back to a branch the next year.
  • Once the ice broke up, people crossed in skiffs, canoes and other small boats until the ferries opened for the season. Some families on the Missouri side waited as long as two weeks for the river to thaw enough to cross.

Far West, Missouri

Then and Now
Between late 1836 and 1839 as many as five thousand Saints made homes in and around Far West. Today farmland surrounds the temple site, which marks the center of what was once a large city.

A County for the Saints
In 1836, three years after the expulsion from Jackson County, the Missouri legislature created Caldwell County in a thinly settled part of the state, meaning it as a place for Latter-day Saints to live. The Saints bought land and laid out Far West on the plat drawn up for the City of Zion.

Headquarters, 1838
Joseph and Emma Smith and their three children arrived on March 14, 1838, and Far West served as Church headquarters until that November. Seven revelations now in the Doctrine and Covenants came to Joseph Smith here, including the law of tithing on July 8.

What Happened Here
  • April 26, 1838: A revelation, now section 115, gave the Church its full name: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. It called Far West "a holy and consecrated land," commanded a temple, and set the Fourth of July as the day to begin.
  • July 4, 1838: Joseph Smith Sr. and a small military unit led a parade to the town square, where the Saints raised a flag on a tall pole and stood around the excavated temple site while workers set the four cornerstones. Thousands watched. Sidney Rigdon gave the day's speech.
  • October 31, 1838: After two weeks of armed fighting in northern Missouri and Governor Lilburn W. Boggs's order to drive the Saints from the state, militia under Major General Samuel D. Lucas surrounded the city. Joseph Smith and other leaders were arrested just outside town and later jailed to await trial. No more work was done on the temple.
  • January 29, 1839: With Joseph in jail, Brigham Young asked the Saints in Far West to covenant to help one another leave the state, and a committee was named to organize it. Most went east to Illinois. By late April only a handful of leaders and a few families were left.
  • April 26, 1839: Section 118 had told the Twelve to leave for England from the temple site on this date. Brigham Young and other apostles rode into the nearly empty town on the moonlit night of April 25, met at the site around daybreak, sang a hymn, and ordained Wilford Woodruff and George A. Smith as apostles.

On the Map
  1. Shoal Creek runs about a mile north of the temple site. The town stood on high rolling prairie between this creek and Goose Creek.
  2. The Far West Temple Site is a fenced plot with a monument and the four cornerstones laid in 1838. The Town
Settled in 1821 on limestone bluffs above the Mississippi, and the Adams County seat from 1825. In the winter of 1838 to 1839 it had about 1,500 people by one Church count and 1,600 by another.

More than 5,000 Latter-day Saints driven out of Missouri came to Quincy that winter. Thousands walked east across the frozen river. Townspeople took families into their homes, found them work, and gathered food, clothing and money.

Quincy was a stopping place. Within about a year most of the Saints had moved some 45 miles north to Commerce, which became Nauvoo.

  • Mid-February 1839: Emma Smith, with Joseph still jailed in Missouri, crossed the frozen Mississippi on foot with her four children. Under her skirt, in cotton bags a friend had sewn, she carried the manuscripts of Joseph's Bible translation. She found lodging with Judge John Cleveland and his wife, Sarah, about four miles from town.
  • February 25 to 28, 1839: The Democratic Association of Quincy met over several days, named a relief committee chaired by J. W. Whitney, and passed resolutions condemning Missouri's treatment of the Saints. The committee set out to feed, clothe and house at least 5,000 people.
  • April 22, 1839: Joseph Smith stepped off a ferry at Quincy after escaping custody in Missouri, in a wide-brimmed hat with his collar turned up. Dimick Huntington recognized him on the bank and took him by back streets to the Cleveland place, where Emma ran out and met him halfway to the gate.

About halfway across Iowa, on the Weldon Fork of the Grand River. Brigham Young and Henry G. Sherwood picked the spot.

  • April 24, 1846: The lead wagons of Brigham Young's company stopped here. Orson Pratt wrote that they "came to a place which we named Garden Grove."

  • May 10, 1846: Garden Grove was organized as a branch, with Samuel Bent as president and David Fullmer and Aaron Johnson as his counselors. Bent was told to divide the land according to need. Brigham Young and the main camp moved on west on May 13.
  • August 16, 1846: Samuel Bent died at Garden Grove. Between 500 and 600 Saints spent the next winter there, and as many as 70 of them died before spring.
  • 1852: The camp kept supplying wagon trains until the last of the Saints left for the Salt Lake Valley. Only a few families stayed behind.

On the Map
  1. The town of Garden Grove stands on or right beside the 1846 camp. A 1979 Church magazine article says the town is on the campsite, while the National Park Service puts the site itself on private farmland nearby. No source pins the exact spot, so the marker shows the middle of town. A brass plaque on a large stone there honors the founders.
  2. The pioneer cemetery is on Mormon Trail Road, just west of town, in a small county park looked after by the Decatur County Conservation Board. It is open to the public.

  • Hosea Stout, who got there a few days after the work started, wrote that the farm went up so fast it seemed a magic city of the woods.

Haun's Mill, Missouri

On Shoal Creek
Jacob Hawn built a gristmill on a bend of Shoal Creek in 1835. He never joined the Church, but he stayed on good terms with the Latter-day Saints who settled around him and worked at his mill.

By 1838
About a dozen cabins and a blacksmith shop stood near the mill, with more Latter-day Saint families farming nearby. Far West, the main settlement of the Saints in Caldwell County, was about 15 miles off.

What Happened Here
  • 1836: Latter-day Saints began moving from Clay County into newly created Caldwell County, and some found land and work near the mill.
  • October 28, 1838: With more families arriving from Ohio and tension rising across northern Missouri, the people at the mill made a peace agreement with the nearby militia.
  • October 30, 1838: An armed mob attacked the settlement in the afternoon. Women and children ran for the woods, and men and boys took shelter in the blacksmith shop. Seventeen Latter-day Saints were killed and more than a dozen wounded. Survivors buried the dead in an unfinished well.
  • November and December 1838: Amanda Barnes Smith lost her husband, Warren, and her son Sardius. Her son Alma was gravely wounded at the hip. She prayed for guidance, cleaned the wound with a mild lye made from fireplace ashes and dressed it with a poultice of slippery elm root. Alma lay still for five weeks and then walked. Because he could not be moved, the family stayed on near the mill through those weeks.
  • Winter of 1838 to 1839: The Saints were forced out of the area and then out of Missouri. Jacob Hawn left as well, and in 1843 he and his wife crossed the plains to Oregon.

On the Map
  1. Haun's Mill lies in woods and fields at the bend of Shoal Creek. The seventeen are buried here. Hawn's house and mill are gone, and there are no trails or benches. Northeast Hauns Mill Drive, the gravel road in, still carries the older spelling.

Notes
  • Church histories long spelled the name "Haun." Jacob Hawn's grave marker in Yamhill, Oregon, reads "Hawn," and newer Church publications use that spelling.
  • A cast-iron face wheel from the mill, dated 1835, lay in the creek bed until a fisherman found it in 1981. Community of Christ gave it to the Church History Museum in Salt Lake City.
  • Community of Christ sold the site to the Church in a purchase made public in May 2012. It is open every day. Heavy rain can flood the roads.

Carthage was the seat of Hancock County and the site of the county jail. Nauvoo, where Joseph Smith was mayor and his brother Hyrum vice mayor, lay about 26 miles to the northwest.

The Jail
Begun in 1839 and finished about two years later, a two-story limestone building with cells for prisoners and rooms for the jailer, George Stigall, and his family. It held mostly people accused of minor crimes.

In June 1844 the Nauvoo city council declared the Nauvoo Expositor a public nuisance and had its press destroyed. Joseph and Hyrum Smith gave themselves up in Carthage on a riot charge, were charged there with treason, and were held in the jail to await trial. They arrived on the evening of June 25.

What Happened Here
  • June 27, 1844: Soon after five in the afternoon, an armed mob stormed the jail and fired into the jailer's upstairs bedroom, where the four men were. Joseph and Hyrum Smith were killed. John Taylor was shot four times and survived; Willard Richards was not hurt. Section 135 of the Doctrine and Covenants, first printed in the 1844 edition, records that they "were shot in Carthage jail, on the 27th of June, 1844, about five o'clock p.m., by an armed mob."
  • May 1845: Five men were tried in Carthage for the killings. The jury acquitted all five.
  • November 5, 1903: The Church bought the jail. It went on serving as a home into the 1930s.
  • 1939: At the urging of Bryant S. Hinckley, president of the Northern States Mission, the Church partly restored the jail and called a missionary couple to give tours.
  • June 27, 1989: President Gordon B. Hinckley dedicated the renovated complex. The jail had been restored as closely as possible to how it looked in 1844, and the visitors' center was enlarged.

On the Map
  1. The courthouse square downtown is listed on the National Register as the Carthage Courthouse Square Historic District.
  2. Hamilton's hotel stood at the southwest corner of Main and Washington Streets, a block south and four blocks east of the jail. Joseph Smith's party stayed there on the night of June 24, 1844. Slate tablets nearby carry quotations from both men.

  • The jail was used as a jail for only about 25 years. After that it was a private house, and one of the nicer ones in Carthage.

The cove itself is Bureau of Land Management land. The Church bought access to it, and to Devil's Gate, from the owners of the neighboring Sun Ranch in 1996, and runs the Mormon Handcart Historic Site from the old ranch headquarters.

What Happened Here
  • October 5, 1856: At Sunday services in Salt Lake City, Brigham Young pleaded for help for the companies still on the plains. Two days later George D. Grant set out with the first relief wagons.
  • October 19, 1856: The Martin company crossed the Platte for the last time, in the first winter storm. Six days later its rations were cut to 8 ounces for adults and 4 for children.
  • November 4, 1856: The company left Devil's Gate in the morning, walked about two miles to the Sweetwater, and crossed that afternoon with the rescuers' help. By John Jaques's account the river was about two feet deep and 30 to 40 yards wide, with ice three or four inches thick. Women and children were carried over first. Wagons took the sick, and some men waded across pulling their own carts. That night they camped in the cove, half a mile past the river.
  • November 9, 1856: The Hunt and Hodgetts companies had emptied their wagons at Fort Seminoe to make room for people who could no longer walk, and the wagons came to the cove to carry them on. Most of the handcarts were left behind.
  • August 15, 1992: President Gordon B. Hinckley dedicated the Martin's Cove Monument. He was back on May 3, 1997 to dedicate the visitors' center at the Sun Ranch.

  2. Fort Seminoe was the abandoned trading post where the wagon companies unloaded. A 2001 survey found the original site in a hayfield near today's visitors' center, and a rebuilt fort now stands close by. The marker shows the rebuilt fort; the sources don't say whether it sits on the exact original spot.
  3. The Sweetwater crossing was about two miles west of the Devil's Gate camp and half a mile below the cove. No account pins down the exact ford, and the marker shows the stretch of river the accounts describe. Carthage, Illinois

County Seat
Carthage was the seat of Hancock County and the site of the county jail. Nauvoo, where Joseph Smith was mayor and his brother Hyrum vice mayor, lay about 26 miles to the northwest.

The Jail
Begun in 1839 and finished about two years later, a two-story limestone building with cells for prisoners and rooms for the jailer, George Stigall, and his family. It held mostly people accused of minor crimes.

Why They Came
In June 1844 the Nauvoo city council declared the Nauvoo Expositor a public nuisance and had its press destroyed. Joseph and Hyrum Smith gave themselves up in Carthage on a riot charge, were charged there with treason, and were held in the jail to await trial. They arrived on the evening of June 25.

What Happened Here
  • June 27, 1844: Soon after five in the afternoon, an armed mob stormed the jail and fired into the jailer's upstairs bedroom, where the four men were. Joseph and Hyrum Smith were killed. John Taylor was shot four times and survived; Willard Richards was not hurt. Section 135 of the Doctrine and Covenants, first printed in the 1844 edition, records that they "were shot in Carthage jail, on the 27th of June, 1844, about five o'clock p.m., by an armed mob."
  • May 1845: Five men were tried in Carthage for the killings. The jury acquitted all five.
  • November 5, 1903: The Church bought the jail. It went on serving as a home into the 1930s.
  • 1939: At the urging of Bryant S. Hinckley, president of the Northern States Mission, the Church partly restored the jail and called a missionary couple to give tours.
  • June 27, 1989: President Gordon B. Hinckley dedicated the renovated complex. The jail had been restored as closely as possible to how it looked in 1844, and the visitors' center was enlarged.

On the Map
  1. The courthouse square downtown is listed on the National Register as the Carthage Courthouse Square Historic District.
  2. Hamilton's hotel stood at the southwest corner of Main and Washington Streets, a block south and four blocks east of the jail. Joseph Smith's party stayed there on the night of June 24, 1844. The next day a hearing on the riot charge was held at the hotel, and that evening the brothers were taken to the jail. Sources give only the street corner, so the marker shows the corner rather than the building itself.
  3. Carthage Jail stands on Walnut Street, a few blocks northwest of the square. Tours start at the visitors' center at 310 Buchanan Street and go through four rooms, two on each floor. On the plaza leading to the jail stands Dee Jay Bawden's statue of the brothers, Hyrum behind Joseph with an arm around him. It was first planned as two separate statues. Slate tablets nearby carry quotations from both men.

Trivia
  • The jail was used as a jail for only about 25 years. After that it was a private house, and one of the nicer ones in Carthage.
  • Building it in 1839 to 1841 cost $4,105. In 1903 the Church paid $4,000 for the jail and its two acres.

- Evan

Mount Pisgah, Iowa

Who Found It
Parley P. Pratt. Riding ahead of his company in May 1846, about 25 miles northwest of Garden Grove, he came on grassy hills crowned with groves above a branch of the Grand River and called out, "This is Mount Pisgah." Pisgah is the height where Moses stood to look over the promised land.

The Second Camp
A way station for Saints who could not yet go on, kept from 1846 to 1852. At its height between 2,000 and 3,000 people lived here. They built homes and two log meetinghouses on a hillside and farmed the fields below.

What Happened Here
  • May 21, 1846: The camp was called together and organized. William Huntington was appointed to preside, with Ezra T. Benson and Charles C. Rich beside him. Plowing started within days.
  • June 26, 1846: Captain James Allen of the U.S. Army rode in to recruit men for a battalion. He met stiff opposition here and was sent on to put the request to Brigham Young at the Missouri.
  • Summer of 1846: Sickness spread through the camp in July and August. At least 80 people died in the settlement's first year. William Huntington was one of them, on August 19.
  • 1852: Church leaders called the remaining Saints in Iowa to gather to Utah, and the settlement was left.
  • May 3, 1886: The Church bought the acre that held the graves. Albert C. White, one of the landowners, had written to President John Taylor suggesting the graves be marked, and Taylor gave the job to Oliver B. Huntington, William's son. Oliver raised donations in Utah and wrote the inscription. The monument was in place by the fall of 1888.

On the Map
  1. The houses stood on the slope east of the cemetery hill, with the fields on the flat land below. Almost nothing of the old camp is left, and the exact layout isn't known; the marker shows the eastern slope where sources place it.
  2. The Mount Pisgah cemetery has the 12-foot marble shaft from 1888. It carries 63 names, though the cemetery likely holds about 150 Latter-day Saints. The Church calls it its first effort to mark its history at the place where it happened. Next to the cemetery is a county park with interpretive markers and a log cabin the Des Moines Iowa Stake built in 1996.

Trivia
  • Brigham Young turned 45 here, on June 1, 1846.
  • Wilford Woodruff was at Mount Pisgah the day Captain Allen arrived. He wrote in his journal that he had "some reasons to believe them to be spies."
  • Parley's brother Orson gave the name a plainer reason. His journal says the Twelve called the place Mount Pisgah because the ground was "more hilly and elevated than the prairies" they had been crossing.

History verified as of October 9, 2026.

  2. The Mount Pisgah cemetery has the 12-foot marble shaft from 1888. It carries 63 names, though the cemetery likely holds about 150 Latter-day Saints. The Church calls it its first effort to mark its history at the place where it happened. Next to the cemetery is a county park with interpretive markers and a log cabin the Des Moines Iowa Stake built in 1996.

Trivia
  • Brigham Young turned 45 here, on June 1, 1846.
  • Wilford Woodruff was at Mount Pisgah the day Captain Allen arrived. He wrote in his journal that he had "some reasons to believe them to be spies."
  • Parley's brother Orson gave the name a plainer reason. His journal says the Twelve called the place Mount Pisgah because the ground was "more hilly and elevated than the prairies" they had been crossing.

Winter Quarters, Nebraska

Whose Land
Land of the Omaha people on the west bank of the Missouri, settled under an agreement with the Omaha and Potawatomi tribes and U.S. Indian agents. The government allowed two years there, so by May 1848 the Saints had to be gone.

That First Winter
About 4,000 people. Another 1,700 Saints wintered in Missouri, mostly in St. Louis, and nearly 3,000 stayed in camps back along the Iowa trail.

The Temple
The Winter Quarters Nebraska Temple, Nebraska's first, went up on the hill on the south side of the pioneer cemetery. President Gordon B. Hinckley dedicated it on April 22, 2001.

What Happened Here
  • September 1846: Surveying started on the 19th, and the first wagons pulled onto the tableland above the river four days later. The plat was a half-size version of Joseph Smith's City of Zion. A December count found 538 log cabins and 83 sod houses.
  • Winter of 1846 to 1847: Food ran short, and scurvy, which the Saints called black canker, spread through the camp along with fever. Hundreds died, mostly the very young and the old.
  • January 14, 1847: Brigham Young received the revelation now in Doctrine and Covenants 136, "the Word and Will of the Lord" for the move west. It set out companies with captains of hundreds, fifties and tens.
  • April 5, 1847: Heber C. Kimball rolled out with the first six wagons. Brigham Young followed on the 7th, and on April 16 the pioneer company organized at its camp on the trail: 143 men, three women and two children, in 72 wagons.
  • July 3, 1848: The last wagons left. With the lease on the Omaha people's land running out, the Saints who were not yet heading west had moved across the river into Iowa and named their new headquarters Kanesville.

On the Map
  1. The town of Winter Quarters filled the flat ground between the bluff and the Missouri, where the Florence neighborhood grew up after the Saints left. The plat ran about a mile along the line of the bluff and a little under half a mile wide. Sources describe the layout but don't fix it to today's streets, so the marker shows only the general area.
  2. The Mormon Pioneer Cemetery is on the bluff just west of the old town, and the temple stands beside it. None of the early gravestones survive. Burial spots were worked out from the sexton's records. Avard Fairbanks's bronze Tragedy at Winter Quarters, in the cemetery, shows two parents who have lost an infant. President Heber J. Grant dedicated it on September 20, 1936. Just east of the cemetery, the Mormon Trail Center at Historic Winter Quarters, on State Street, was dedicated by President Hinckley on April 18, 1997. Its exhibits include a model of the 1846 settlement, and visitors can pull a handcart.

Trivia
  • Nobody is sure how many died. Thomas L. Kane said in 1850 there were "something over 600" burials. A later study of the sexton's records estimated about 323 in this cemetery and roughly 433 across the camps' three burial grounds.
  • Omaha leased the cemetery to the Church for $1 a year from the mid-1930s. On April 1, 1999, the mayor deeded it over outright, for another dollar.
  • After the Saints left, James C. Mitchell laid out a new town on the site and called it Florence. Omaha annexed it in 1917. The neighborhood still goes by Florence, and its 1856 Bank of Florence stands on North 30th Street.

History verified as of October 9, 2026.
